## Objectives {#objectifs}

This module provides the language in which the internship frames its questions: a physical model is a **dynamical system** $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = F_{\boldsymbol\lambda}(\mathbf{x})$, its regimes change at **bifurcations** when a parameter $\boldsymbol\lambda$ (here $Rm$, $\Gamma$…) crosses a threshold, and what a generative model must learn is not a trajectory, which is unpredictable beyond a few characteristic times, but the **invariant measure** $\mu_{\boldsymbol\lambda}$ that describes the statistics of the regime. By the end of the planned twenty-five hours, you will be able to:

1. state the Cauchy–Lipschitz theorem, prove Grönwall's lemma and the group property of the flow, and compute how a flow transports volumes (Liouville's formula);
2. find the fixed points of a system, classify them by the eigenvalues of the Jacobian, and prove stability with a Lyapunov function;
3. recognize the saddle-node, pitchfork (super- and subcritical) and Hopf bifurcations from their normal forms, explain why the symmetry $\mathbf{B} \mapsto -\mathbf{B}$ makes the pitchfork generic, and prove the amplitude law $\sqrt{R - R_c}$ and the bistability boundary $27h^2 = 4r^3$ of the imperfect pitchfork;
4. compute numerically the Lyapunov exponents of the Lorenz system, relate their sum to the divergence of the vector field, and describe the merging crisis of two symmetric attractors that gives rise to reversals;
5. define invariant measure, ergodicity and physical (SRB) measure, write the Liouville and Fokker–Planck equations, and **prove** the stationarity identities $\mathbb{E}_\mu[F\cdot\nabla\varphi + \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}\Delta\varphi] = 0$, of which the energy budget is a special case;
6. explain why these identities do not fix the relative weight of two symmetric attractors (convexity of the set of invariant measures, ergodic measures as extreme points);
7. prove the mean first-passage time formula in dimension 1, derive the Arrhenius–Kramers law from it, and estimate a reversal frequency with the Rice formula $\mathbb{E}[|\dot X|\,\delta(X)]$ from the stationary distribution alone;
8. reproduce, on the three-mode model of Gissinger (2012), the reversal threshold, the stationarity identities and the Rice formula used in experiment E1 of the repository.

## Prerequisites {#prerequis}

The starting point is the level of the second year of a French undergraduate degree (L2). You should be able to differentiate a function of several variables, compute a Jacobian matrix, diagonalize a $2\times 2$ or $3\times 3$ matrix (real or complex eigenvalues), solve a linear differential equation with constant coefficients, and know the basics of probability: expectation, variance, density, Gaussian distribution, exponential distribution. Chapters 5 and 6 use Brownian motion heuristically; no prior knowledge of stochastic calculus is assumed.

On the programming side, it is enough to handle NumPy arrays and write a loop; SciPy is used for `solve_ivp` (integration of differential equations) and `quad` (integrals). Three interactive diagrams, which compute directly in your browser, accompany chapters 3, 6 and 7.

The module [Vector calculus and Fourier analysis](../p1-calcul-vectoriel/index.html) provides the operators $\nabla\cdot$ and $\Delta$ and the integration by parts used in chapter 5. The module [Electromagnetism, MHD and the dynamo effect](../p3-mhd-dynamo/index.html) gives the physics of reversals; it can be read in parallel. This module then feeds directly into the modules [Probability, statistics and optimal transport](../p5-probabilites-transport/index.html) (distributions, distances between distributions), [Generative models: diffusion and flow matching](../p7-modeles-generatifs/index.html) (the flow of a vector field, the continuity equation) and [Generative models under physical constraints](../p8-contraintes-physiques/index.html) (the stationarity identities as a constraint “in distribution”).

## 1. Autonomous equations, flow and phase portraits {#ch1}

The models of the internship, from Gissinger's three-mode oscillator to the MHD equations discretized on a grid of several million points, all have the same form: the state at a given instant entirely determines its rate of change. This chapter sets out the vocabulary (vector field, orbit, flow), the theorem that guarantees that a simulation makes sense (Cauchy–Lipschitz), and the formula that tells how a flow deforms volumes, the starting point of the whole theory of invariant measures.

### 1.1 Vector field, solutions, orbits

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Autonomous dynamical system]{.tag}
Let $F : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be a function of class $C^1$, called a **vector field**. The associated autonomous differential system is

$$
\dot{\mathbf{x}}(t) = F(\mathbf{x}(t)), \qquad \mathbf{x}(0) = \mathbf{x}_0 .
$$

A **solution** is a function $\mathbf{x}$ of class $C^1$ on an interval containing $0$ that satisfies the equation. The space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the **phase space**; the set of points $\{\mathbf{x}(t)\}$ visited by a solution is its **orbit**. “Autonomous” means that $F$ does not depend explicitly on time. The dimension of the state is denoted $n$ in this module (it is denoted $D$ in the other modules; here, $D$ stands for the dipole of the Gissinger model).
:::

::: note
[Remark 1.2 — Everything reduces to this form]{.tag}
A second-order equation such as that of the pendulum, $\ddot\theta = -\sin\theta$, becomes a first-order system by setting $\mathbf{x} = (\theta, \omega)$ with $\dot\theta = \omega$ and $\dot\omega = -\sin\theta$. A non-autonomous system $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = F(\mathbf{x}, t)$ becomes autonomous by adding time as a variable: $\dot\tau = 1$. Finally, a partial differential equation such as the induction equation, once discretized in space (finite differences, finite elements, Fourier), is a system of this type with $n$ equal to the number of unknowns.
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.3 — The three systems that recur in this module]{.tag}
*(a)* The **damped oscillator** $\ddot x + \gamma\dot x + x = 0$, i.e. $F(x, y) = (y, -x - \gamma y)$.

*(b)* The **Lorenz system** (1963), a three-mode truncation of thermal convection:

$$
\dot x = s\,(y - x), \qquad \dot y = x\,(r - z) - y, \qquad \dot z = xy - b\,z ,
$$

with the classical values $s = 10$ (Prandtl number, often denoted $\sigma$; here $\sigma$ is reserved for noise), $b = 8/3$ and $r = 28$.

*(c)* The **Gissinger model** (2012), a three-mode model of magnetic field reversals, with the quadrupole $Q$, the dipole $D$ and a velocity mode $V$:

$$
\dot Q = \mu Q - V D, \qquad \dot D = -\nu D + V Q, \qquad \dot V = \Gamma - V + Q D .
$$

We set $\mu = 0.119$ and $\nu = 0.1$ as in Gissinger (2012); $\Gamma$ is the control parameter. This model is the common thread of the module and is the subject of chapter 7.
:::

### 1.2 Existence, uniqueness and continuous dependence

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.4 — Cauchy–Lipschitz]{.tag}
If $F$ is locally Lipschitz (which is the case if $F$ is of class $C^1$), then for every $\mathbf{x}_0$ there exists a unique maximal solution, defined on an open interval $\left]T_-, T_+\right[$ containing $0$. Moreover, if $T_+ < \infty$, then $|\mathbf{x}(t)| \to \infty$ as $t \to T_+$: a solution can stop in finite time only by blowing up.

::: proof
Sketch. We rewrite the problem in integral form, $\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{x}_0 + \int_0^t F(\mathbf{x}(\tau))\,\mathrm{d}\tau$. On an interval $[0, \tau_0]$ short enough that $L\tau_0 < 1$ ($L$ a Lipschitz constant of $F$ near $\mathbf{x}_0$), the map $\mathbf{x} \mapsto \mathbf{x}_0 + \int_0^t F(\mathbf{x})$ is a contraction for the maximum norm, and the Banach fixed-point theorem gives local existence and uniqueness (Picard iterations). The local solutions are then glued together; global uniqueness follows from proposition 1.6 below. If the solution remained bounded near $T_+$, it could be extended beyond it, which would contradict maximality. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Lemma 1.5 — Grönwall]{.tag}
Let $u$ be a continuous nonnegative function on $[0, T]$ such that $u(t) \le a + L\int_0^t u(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau$ for all $t$, with $a \ge 0$ and $L \ge 0$. Then $u(t) \le a\,e^{Lt}$.

::: proof
Let $w(t) = a + L\int_0^t u$. Then $w' = Lu \le Lw$, so $(w\,e^{-Lt})' = (w' - Lw)\,e^{-Lt} \le 0$, and $w(t)\,e^{-Lt} \le w(0) = a$. We conclude using $u \le w$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.6 — Continuous dependence on initial conditions]{.tag}
If $F$ is $L$-Lipschitz on a region that contains two solutions $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ up to time $T$, then for $0 \le t \le T$:

$$
|\mathbf{x}(t) - \mathbf{y}(t)| \le |\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{y}_0|\,e^{Lt}.
$$

::: proof
By the integral form, $\mathbf{x}(t) - \mathbf{y}(t) = \mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{y}_0 + \int_0^t \big(F(\mathbf{x}) - F(\mathbf{y})\big)$, so $|\mathbf{x}(t) - \mathbf{y}(t)| \le |\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{y}_0| + L\int_0^t |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}|$. Grönwall's lemma concludes. With $\mathbf{x}_0 = \mathbf{y}_0$, we obtain uniqueness. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

This bound says that two nearby solutions remain close **for a finite time**. It does not prevent the separation from growing exponentially: this is exactly what happens in a chaotic system (chapter 4), where the factor $e^{Lt}$ is replaced by $e^{\lambda_1 t}$, with $\lambda_1$ the Lyapunov exponent.

::: ex
[Example 1.7 — Blow-up and non-uniqueness]{.tag}
The equation $\dot x = x^2$ has the solution $x(t) = x_0/(1 - x_0 t)$, which blows up at time $T_+ = 1/x_0$ if $x_0 > 0$: $F$ is $C^1$ but not globally Lipschitz. The equation $\dot x = 2\sqrt{|x|}$, with $x(0) = 0$, on the other hand admits two solutions, $x \equiv 0$ and $x(t) = t^2$ for $t \ge 0$: the square root is not Lipschitz at $0$, and uniqueness fails (exercise 2).
:::

For the systems of this module, blow-up is ruled out by an energy argument: we will show in chapter 4 that Lorenz trajectories enter an ellipsoid and never leave it. A solution that stays in a compact set is defined for all $t \ge 0$, by the second part of theorem 1.4.

### 1.3 The flow and the transport of volumes

::: def
[Definition 1.8 — Flow]{.tag}
The **flow** of $F$ is the map $\Phi^t$ that sends an initial condition to the value at time $t$ of the solution starting from it: $\Phi^t(\mathbf{x}_0) = \mathbf{x}(t)$. The flow is denoted $\Phi$ (capital letter) to reserve $\varphi$ for the test functions of chapter 5.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.9 — Group property]{.tag}
We have $\Phi^0 = \mathrm{Id}$ and $\Phi^{t+s} = \Phi^t \circ \Phi^s$ wherever these quantities are defined. In particular, $\Phi^t$ is invertible, with inverse $\Phi^{-t}$.

::: proof
Fix $s$ and $\mathbf{x}_0$. The two functions $t \mapsto \Phi^{t+s}(\mathbf{x}_0)$ and $t \mapsto \Phi^t(\Phi^s(\mathbf{x}_0))$ are solutions of $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = F(\mathbf{x})$ (for the first one, because $F$ does not depend on time: a time-shifted solution is still a solution) and both equal $\Phi^s(\mathbf{x}_0)$ at $t = 0$. By uniqueness, they coincide. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.10 — Variational equation and Liouville's formula]{.tag}
Let $M(t) = D\Phi^t(\mathbf{x}_0)$ denote the Jacobian matrix of the flow with respect to the initial condition. It satisfies the **variational equation**

$$
\dot M(t) = DF(\mathbf{x}(t))\,M(t), \qquad M(0) = I,
$$

and its determinant is

$$
\det M(t) = \exp\Big(\int_0^t \nabla\cdot F(\mathbf{x}(\tau))\,\mathrm{d}\tau\Big). \tag{1.1}
$$

Consequently, for every region $A$ of phase space, $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\operatorname{vol}\big(\Phi^t(A)\big) = \int_{\Phi^t(A)} \nabla\cdot F\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}$.

::: proof
We assume that $\Phi^t$ is differentiable with respect to $\mathbf{x}_0$ (this holds for $F$ of class $C^1$). Differentiating $\partial_t\Phi^t(\mathbf{x}_0) = F(\Phi^t(\mathbf{x}_0))$ with respect to $\mathbf{x}_0$ and exchanging the derivatives, we obtain the variational equation. Jacobi's formula for the derivative of a determinant then gives $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\det M = \det M\cdot\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1}\dot M) = \det M\cdot\operatorname{tr}\big(DF(\mathbf{x}(t))\big)$, and the trace of the Jacobian is the divergence: $\operatorname{tr} DF = \nabla\cdot F$. Integrating this scalar linear equation yields (1.1). For the volume, the change of variables $\mathbf{x} = \Phi^t(\mathbf{x}_0)$ gives $\operatorname{vol}(\Phi^t(A)) = \int_A \det M(t, \mathbf{x}_0)\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_0$; we differentiate under the integral sign and change variables back. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 1.11 — Conservative system, dissipative system]{.tag}
A system is **conservative** if $\nabla\cdot F = 0$: its flow preserves volumes (Hamiltonian systems, ideal fluid). It is **dissipative** if $\nabla\cdot F < 0$: phase-space volumes contract.
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.12 — Two dissipative systems]{.tag}
For Lorenz, $\nabla\cdot F = \partial_x[s(y - x)] + \partial_y[x(r - z) - y] + \partial_z[xy - bz] = -(s + 1 + b) = -41/3 \approx -13.67$, a constant. By (1.1), every volume is multiplied by $e^{-13.67} \approx 1.2\times 10^{-6}$ in one time unit. For Gissinger, $\nabla\cdot F = \mu - \nu - 1 = -0.981$. In both cases, the set toward which trajectories converge has zero volume: we will meet this property again in chapter 5, where it prevents the stationary distribution from having a density.
:::

The following code checks numerically the group property, formula (1.1) and continuous dependence on the Lorenz system.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

s, r, b = 10.0, 28.0, 8.0 / 3.0       # Prandtl number s, reduced Rayleigh number r, geometric factor b

def lorenz(t, x):
    return [s * (x[1] - x[0]), x[0] * (r - x[2]) - x[1], x[0] * x[1] - b * x[2]]

def jacobienne(x):
    return np.array([[-s, s, 0.0],
                     [r - x[2], -1.0, -x[0]],
                     [x[1], x[0], -b]])

def flot(x0, t):
    """phi_t(x0), computed with a very tight tolerance."""
    sol = solve_ivp(lorenz, (0.0, t), x0, method="DOP853", rtol=1e-12, atol=1e-12)
    return sol.y[:, -1]

x0 = np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0])

# 1) Group property: phi_{1.5} = phi_1 o phi_{0.5}
ecart = np.abs(flot(x0, 1.5) - flot(flot(x0, 0.5), 1.0)).max()
print(f"|phi_1.5(x0) - phi_1(phi_0.5(x0))| = {ecart:.1e}")

# 2) Variational equation dM/dt = DF(x(t)) M, M(0) = I, then Liouville's formula
def etendu(t, y):
    x, M = y[:3], y[3:].reshape(3, 3)
    return np.concatenate([lorenz(t, x), (jacobienne(x) @ M).ravel()])

div = -(s + 1.0 + b)
for T in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0):
    sol = solve_ivp(etendu, (0.0, T), np.concatenate([x0, np.eye(3).ravel()]),
                    method="DOP853", rtol=1e-12, atol=1e-14)
    M = sol.y[3:, -1].reshape(3, 3)
    print(f"T = {T:3.1f} : det M(T) = {np.linalg.det(M):.6e} ; exp(T div F) = {np.exp(T * div):.6e}")

# 3) Continuous dependence (Grönwall): two initial conditions 1e-8 apart
y0 = x0 + np.array([1e-8, 0.0, 0.0])
for T in (1.0, 10.0, 20.0, 30.0):
    print(f"T = {T:4.1f} : |phi_T(x0) - phi_T(y0)| = {np.linalg.norm(flot(x0, T) - flot(y0, T)):.2e}")
# output:
# |phi_1.5(x0) - phi_1(phi_0.5(x0))| = 2.2e-13
# T = 0.5 : det M(T) = 1.077261e-03 ; exp(T div F) = 1.077261e-03
# T = 1.0 : det M(T) = 1.160492e-06 ; exp(T div F) = 1.160492e-06
# T = 2.0 : det M(T) = 1.346777e-12 ; exp(T div F) = 1.346741e-12
# T =  1.0 : |phi_T(x0) - phi_T(y0)| = 1.12e-08
# T = 10.0 : |phi_T(x0) - phi_T(y0)| = 1.76e-08
# T = 20.0 : |phi_T(x0) - phi_T(y0)| = 9.25e-06
# T = 30.0 : |phi_T(x0) - phi_T(y0)| = 2.21e-01
```

The discrepancy of $2\times 10^{-13}$ is the integration error: the group property holds. The determinant follows $e^{t\,\nabla\cdot F}$ to six digits; at time $2$, the relative discrepancy of $3\times 10^{-5}$ comes from the absolute tolerance of the integrator ($10^{-14}$ on entries of $M$ of order $1$), which is coarse on the scale of a determinant of $10^{-12}$ obtained through cancellations. Finally, the initial separation of $10^{-8}$ remains small until $t = 10$, then becomes of order $1$ around $t = 30$: the dependence is continuous at fixed time, but the amplification is exponential, as we will quantify in chapter 4.

### 1.4 Phase portraits in dimensions 1 and 2

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.13 — In dimension 1, no oscillation]{.tag}
For $\dot x = f(x)$ with $f$ of class $C^1$ on $\mathbb{R}$, every solution is monotone. A bounded solution converges to a zero of $f$.

::: proof
If $f(x_0) = 0$, the solution is constant. Otherwise, $f(x(t))$ cannot vanish: if $f(x(t_1)) = 0$, the constant solution equal to $x(t_1)$ and our solution would coincide at $t_1$, hence everywhere by uniqueness, which contradicts $f(x_0) \neq 0$. Thus $\dot x$ keeps a constant sign and $x$ is monotone. If it is bounded, it has a limit $\ell$; if we had $f(\ell) \neq 0$, we would have $\dot x \to f(\ell) \neq 0$ and $x$ could not converge. Hence $f(\ell) = 0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The phase portrait of a scalar equation can therefore be read off the sign of $f$: mark its zeros on the line and draw an arrow to the right where $f > 0$, to the left where $f < 0$. A zero toward which the arrows converge is stable; a zero they flee from is unstable. Interactive diagram 1 (chapter 3) applies this method to the normal forms.

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.14 — Poincaré–Bendixson (statement)]{.tag}
In the plane, if a forward orbit stays in a compact set that contains no fixed point, then its limit set is a periodic orbit: either the orbit is itself periodic, or it winds onto a periodic orbit (a limit cycle).

::: proof
Stated without proof; see Strogatz (2018) or Guckenheimer and Holmes (1983). The idea is that a curve in the plane that does not intersect itself (uniqueness) is trapped by the Jordan curve theorem. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

An important consequence: **a two-dimensional autonomous system cannot be chaotic**. At least three variables are needed, which is why the minimal models of Lorenz and Gissinger have exactly three.

::: ex
[Example 1.15 — Damped pendulum]{.tag}
For $\dot\theta = \omega$, $\dot\omega = -\sin\theta - \gamma\omega$ with $\gamma = 0.5$, the fixed points are $(k\pi, 0)$. The nullclines are the line $\omega = 0$ (where $\dot\theta = 0$) and the curve $\omega = -\sin(\theta)/\gamma$ (where $\dot\omega = 0$). The energy $E = \omega^2/2 - \cos\theta$ decreases along trajectories, since $\dot E = \omega\dot\omega + \sin\theta\,\dot\theta = -\gamma\omega^2 \le 0$. Trajectories spiral toward the points $(2k\pi, 0)$, the lower positions of the pendulum; the points $((2k+1)\pi, 0)$, the upper positions, are saddles. Chapter 2 explains how to read these types off the eigenvalues.
:::

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 1
:::
- An autonomous system $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = F(\mathbf{x})$ with $F$ of class $C^1$ has a unique maximal solution (Cauchy–Lipschitz), which can only be interrupted by blow-up.
- Grönwall: $|\mathbf{x}(t) - \mathbf{y}(t)| \le |\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{y}_0|\,e^{Lt}$; the dependence is continuous, but the amplification can be exponential.
- The flow satisfies $\Phi^{t+s} = \Phi^t\circ\Phi^s$; its Jacobian obeys $\dot M = DF\,M$ and $\det M(t) = \exp\int_0^t \nabla\cdot F$ (Liouville).
- Lorenz ($\nabla\cdot F = -41/3$) and Gissinger ($\nabla\cdot F = \mu - \nu - 1$) contract volumes.
- In dimension 1, solutions are monotone; in dimension 2, there is no chaos (Poincaré–Bendixson); $n \ge 3$ is needed.
::::

## 2. Fixed points, linearization and stability {#ch2}

A dynamo threshold is the point at which the state without a magnetic field, $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{0}$, ceases to be stable: computing it means carrying out a linear stability analysis. Experiment E3 of the repository thus measures the growth rate of the kinematic ABC dynamo as a function of $Rm$, that is, the largest real part of the eigenvalues of the linearized induction operator (see the [report](../../rapport/index.html#e3)). This chapter provides the tools for this analysis in finite dimension.

### 2.1 Fixed points and notions of stability

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Fixed point, stability]{.tag}
A **fixed point** (or equilibrium point) is a point $\mathbf{x}^*$ such that $F(\mathbf{x}^*) = \mathbf{0}$: the solution starting from it is constant. It is

- **stable** (in the sense of Lyapunov) if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $|\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{x}^*| < \delta$ implies $|\Phi^t(\mathbf{x}_0) - \mathbf{x}^*| < \varepsilon$ for all $t \ge 0$;
- **asymptotically stable** if it is stable and, in addition, $\Phi^t(\mathbf{x}_0) \to \mathbf{x}^*$ for $\mathbf{x}_0$ close enough;
- **unstable** if it is not stable.
:::

### 2.2 Linear systems

For $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = A\mathbf{x}$ with $A$ a constant matrix, the solution is $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{tA}\mathbf{x}_0$, where $e^{tA} = \sum_k t^k A^k / k!$. If $A = P\Lambda P^{-1}$ is diagonalizable, $e^{tA} = P\,e^{t\Lambda}P^{-1}$: each eigenmode evolves as $e^{\lambda_k t}$, and the real part of $\lambda_k$ determines its growth or decay.

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.2 — Stability of a linear system]{.tag}
The origin is asymptotically stable for $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = A\mathbf{x}$ if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ have a strictly negative real part. If one of them has a strictly positive real part, the origin is unstable.

::: proof
Diagonalizable case. Let $\alpha = \max_k \operatorname{Re}\lambda_k$. Then $|e^{tA}\mathbf{x}_0| \le \|P\|\,\|P^{-1}\|\,e^{\alpha t}|\mathbf{x}_0|$, which tends to $0$ if $\alpha < 0$, and which is small uniformly in $t$ if $|\mathbf{x}_0|$ is small: asymptotic stability. If $\operatorname{Re}\lambda_k > 0$, the solution starting from $\varepsilon\,\mathbf{v}_k$ (an eigenvector, or the real part of a complex eigenvector) grows as $e^{t\operatorname{Re}\lambda_k}$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$: instability. In the general case, the Jordan form brings in terms $t^m e^{\lambda t}$, and the same conclusion holds with $\alpha$ replaced by any $\alpha' > \alpha$. If all the real parts are $\le 0$ and one of them is zero, the corresponding mode does not decay: there is no asymptotic stability. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

In dimension 2, the eigenvalues depend only on the trace $\tau = \operatorname{tr}A$ and the determinant $\Delta = \det A$: $\lambda = \big(\tau \pm \sqrt{\tau^2 - 4\Delta}\big)/2$. This yields the following classification.

| Condition | Eigenvalues | Type of the origin |
|---|---|---|
| $\Delta < 0$ | real, of opposite signs | saddle (always unstable) |
| $\Delta > 0$, $\tau^2 > 4\Delta$ | real, of the same sign | node, stable if $\tau < 0$ |
| $\Delta > 0$, $\tau^2 < 4\Delta$ | complex conjugate | focus (spiral), stable if $\tau < 0$ |
| $\Delta > 0$, $\tau = 0$ | purely imaginary | center (closed orbits) |

::: ex
[Example 2.3 — Damped oscillator]{.tag}
For $\ddot x + \gamma\dot x + x = 0$, we have $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & -\gamma\end{pmatrix}$, hence $\tau = -\gamma$ and $\Delta = 1$. For $0 < \gamma < 2$, $\tau^2 < 4\Delta$: the origin is a stable focus, and the oscillation decays as $e^{-\gamma t/2}$. For $\gamma > 2$, it is a stable node (overdamped regime). For $\gamma = 0$, it is a center.
:::

### 2.3 Linearization around a fixed point

Near a fixed point, we write $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}^* + \mathbf{y}$ and $F(\mathbf{x}^* + \mathbf{y}) = A\mathbf{y} + R(\mathbf{y})$, with $A = DF(\mathbf{x}^*)$ and a remainder $|R(\mathbf{y})| \le C|\mathbf{y}|^2$ if $F$ is of class $C^2$.

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.4 — Linearized stability]{.tag}
If all the eigenvalues of $A = DF(\mathbf{x}^*)$ have a strictly negative real part, $\mathbf{x}^*$ is asymptotically stable, and the convergence is exponential. If one of them has a strictly positive real part, $\mathbf{x}^*$ is unstable.

::: proof
First claim. Since the eigenvalues of $A$ have negative real parts, the integral $P = \int_0^\infty e^{tA^{\mathsf T}}e^{tA}\,\mathrm{d}t$ converges (theorem 2.2). The matrix $P$ is symmetric positive definite, and by integrating $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\big(e^{tA^{\mathsf T}}e^{tA}\big) = A^{\mathsf T}e^{tA^{\mathsf T}}e^{tA} + e^{tA^{\mathsf T}}e^{tA}A$ from $0$ to $\infty$, we find the **Lyapunov equation** $A^{\mathsf T}P + PA = -I$. Let $V(\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{y}^{\mathsf T}P\mathbf{y}$. Along a solution,

$$
\dot V = \mathbf{y}^{\mathsf T}(A^{\mathsf T}P + PA)\,\mathbf{y} + 2\,\mathbf{y}^{\mathsf T}P\,R(\mathbf{y}) \le -|\mathbf{y}|^2 + 2\|P\|\,C\,|\mathbf{y}|^3 .
$$

For $|\mathbf{y}| \le \rho_0 = 1/(4\|P\|C)$, we therefore have $\dot V \le -|\mathbf{y}|^2/2 \le -V/(2\lambda_{\max}(P))$. Choose $c = \lambda_{\min}(P)\,\rho_0^2$: the set $\{V \le c\}$ is contained in the ball of radius $\rho_0$, and since $V$ decreases there, a solution starting in this set cannot leave it. Along such a solution, $V$ decreases exponentially; since $V \ge \lambda_{\min}(P)|\mathbf{y}|^2$, so does $\mathbf{y}$. The second claim (instability) is proved with a similar construction; we omit it. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Remark 2.5 — Hyperbolic points, Hartman–Grobman theorem]{.tag}
A fixed point is **hyperbolic** if no eigenvalue of $DF(\mathbf{x}^*)$ has zero real part. The Hartman–Grobman theorem (stated without proof) states that in a neighborhood of a hyperbolic point, the phase portrait is a continuous deformation of that of the linearized system. When an eigenvalue has zero real part, linearization is inconclusive: this is precisely the situation of **bifurcations** (chapter 3).
:::

::: ex
[Example 2.6 — The fixed points of Lorenz]{.tag}
The origin is always a fixed point. At $O$, the Jacobian has eigenvalues $-b$ and the roots of $\lambda^2 + (s + 1)\lambda + s(1 - r) = 0$. For $r < 1$, all are negative: $O$ is stable. For $r > 1$, the product of the roots $s(1 - r)$ is negative, so one of them is positive: $O$ becomes a saddle. At the same time, two symmetric fixed points $C_\pm = \big(\pm\sqrt{b(r-1)}, \pm\sqrt{b(r-1)}, r - 1\big)$ appear, stable as long as $r < r_H = s(s + b + 3)/(s - b - 1) \approx 24.74$ (formula stated without proof; we check it numerically below). At $r = 28$, all three fixed points are unstable, and yet trajectories remain bounded (proposition 4.1): apart from the exceptional ones that land exactly on the stable manifold of a fixed point, they converge to no equilibrium and oscillate indefinitely, periodically or chaotically.
:::

::: ex
[Example 2.7 — The fixed points of the Gissinger model]{.tag}
The point $O = (0, 0, \Gamma)$ is fixed. The Jacobian at a point $(Q, D, V)$ is

$$
DF = \begin{pmatrix} \mu & -V & -D \\ V & -\nu & Q \\ D & Q & -1 \end{pmatrix},
$$

which at $O$ consists of a block $\begin{pmatrix} \mu & -\Gamma \\ \Gamma & -\nu \end{pmatrix}$ followed by the eigenvalue $-1$. The block has trace $\mu - \nu$ and determinant $\Gamma^2 - \mu\nu$, hence $\lambda_{1,2} = \frac{\mu - \nu}{2} \pm \frac12\sqrt{(\mu + \nu)^2 - 4\Gamma^2}$ (Gissinger, 2012). With $\mu = 0.119$, $\nu = 0.1$ and $\Gamma = 0.9$, we get $0.0095 \pm 0.893\,i$: $O$ is a **barely unstable** focus, and the amplitude of an oscillation around $O$ only doubles in $\ln 2/0.0095 \approx 73$ time units.

For the other fixed points, we combine $\mu Q = VD$ and $\nu D = VQ$: if $QD \ne 0$, we get $\mu\nu\,QD = V^2\,QD$, hence $V = \pm\sqrt{\mu\nu}$. With $V = -\sqrt{\mu\nu}$, the equation $\dot V = 0$ gives $Q^2 = \nu + \Gamma\sqrt{\nu/\mu}$ and $D = -Q\sqrt{\mu/\nu}$: these are the points $N_\pm$, which always exist. With $V = +\sqrt{\mu\nu}$, we get $Q^2 = \nu - \Gamma\sqrt{\nu/\mu}$, positive only if $\sqrt{\mu\nu} > \Gamma$: these points $M_\pm$ do not exist here, since $\sqrt{\mu\nu} \approx 0.109 < 0.9$.
:::

The following code computes these eigenvalues and locates numerically the Hopf bifurcation of Lorenz.

```python
import numpy as np

# --- Lorenz: origin and C+ = (a, a, r - 1), a = sqrt(b (r - 1)) ---
s, b = 10.0, 8.0 / 3.0

def jac_lorenz(x, r):
    return np.array([[-s, s, 0.0], [r - x[2], -1.0, -x[0]], [x[1], x[0], -b]])

for r in (0.5, 10.0, 28.0):
    vp0 = np.linalg.eigvals(jac_lorenz(np.zeros(3), r))
    texte = f"r = {r:4.1f} : max Re(eig) at O = {vp0.real.max():+.3f}"
    if r > 1:
        a = np.sqrt(b * (r - 1))
        vpC = np.linalg.eigvals(jac_lorenz(np.array([a, a, r - 1]), r))
        texte += f" ; at C+ = {vpC.real.max():+.3f}"
    print(texte)

# Hopf threshold of C+: sweep in r, compared with the closed-form formula
rs = np.arange(20.0, 30.0, 0.01)
mx = np.array([np.linalg.eigvals(jac_lorenz(np.array([np.sqrt(b*(r-1))]*2 + [r-1]), r)).real.max()
               for r in rs])
r_num = rs[np.argmax(mx > 0)]
print(f"numerical Hopf r_H ≈ {r_num:.2f} ; formula s(s+b+3)/(s-b-1) = "
      f"{s * (s + b + 3) / (s - b - 1):.4f}")

# --- Gissinger (2012): mu = 0.119, nu = 0.1, Gamma = 0.9 ---
mu, nu, G = 0.119, 0.1, 0.9

def jac_giss(x):
    q, d, v = x
    return np.array([[mu, -v, -d], [v, -nu, q], [d, q, -1.0]])

O = np.array([0.0, 0.0, G])
print("O  : eigenvalues", np.round(np.linalg.eigvals(jac_giss(O)), 4))
print("     formula: (mu-nu)/2 ± i sqrt(4G^2-(mu+nu)^2)/2 =",
      f"{(mu-nu)/2:.4f} ± {np.sqrt(4*G**2-(mu+nu)**2)/2:.4f} i")
print("M± exist?", np.sqrt(mu * nu) > G, f"(sqrt(mu nu) = {np.sqrt(mu*nu):.4f})")
q = np.sqrt(nu + G * np.sqrt(nu / mu)); d = -np.sqrt(mu + G * np.sqrt(mu / nu)); v = -np.sqrt(mu * nu)
Np = np.array([q, d, v])
F = np.array([mu*q - v*d, -nu*d + v*q, G - v + q*d])
print("N+ =", np.round(Np, 4), "; |F(N+)| =", f"{np.abs(F).max():.1e}")
print("N+ : eigenvalues", np.round(np.linalg.eigvals(jac_giss(Np)), 4))
print("divergence mu - nu - 1 =", round(mu - nu - 1, 3))
# output:
# r =  0.5 : max Re(eig) at O = -0.475
# r = 10.0 : max Re(eig) at O = +5.466 ; at C+ = -0.595
# r = 28.0 : max Re(eig) at O = +11.828 ; at C+ = +0.094
# numerical Hopf r_H ≈ 24.74 ; formula s(s+b+3)/(s-b-1) = 24.7368
# O  : eigenvalues [ 0.0095+0.8933j  0.0095-0.8933j -1.    +0.j    ]
#      formula: (mu-nu)/2 ± i sqrt(4G^2-(mu+nu)^2)/2 = 0.0095 ± 0.8933 i
# M± exist? False (sqrt(mu nu) = 0.1091)
# N+ = [ 0.9618 -1.0492 -0.1091] ; |F(N+)| = 1.4e-17
# N+ : eigenvalues [-1.1691+0.j      0.094 +0.6065j  0.094 -0.6065j]
# divergence mu - nu - 1 = -0.981
```

The threshold $r_H$ found by the sweep agrees with the formula. For the Gissinger model, the formula for the eigenvalues at $O$ is confirmed, and $N_+$ has a pair of complex eigenvalues with real part $+0.094$: it is an unstable **saddle-focus**, which attracts in one direction ($-1.17$) and repels in a spiral in the other two. Trajectories remain bounded (Gissinger, 2012, attributes this to the relative signs of the quadratic terms; we observe it numerically). Since all the fixed points are unstable, a typical trajectory converges to no equilibrium and oscillates indefinitely; we will see that it is chaotic.

### 2.4 Lyapunov functions

Linearization says nothing far from the fixed point, nor in non-hyperbolic cases. Lyapunov's direct method generalizes the idea of a decreasing energy.

::: def
[Definition 2.8 — Lyapunov function]{.tag}
Let $U$ be a neighborhood of $\mathbf{x}^*$. A function $V : U \to \mathbb{R}$ of class $C^1$ is a **Lyapunov function** if $V(\mathbf{x}^*) = 0$, $V(\mathbf{x}) > 0$ for $\mathbf{x} \ne \mathbf{x}^*$, and $\dot V(\mathbf{x}) = \nabla V(\mathbf{x})\cdot F(\mathbf{x}) \le 0$ on $U$. It is **strict** if $\dot V < 0$ on $U \setminus\{\mathbf{x}^*\}$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.9 — Lyapunov's direct method]{.tag}
If there exists a Lyapunov function, $\mathbf{x}^*$ is stable; if it is strict, $\mathbf{x}^*$ is asymptotically stable. If moreover $U = \mathbb{R}^n$ and $V(\mathbf{x}) \to \infty$ as $|\mathbf{x}| \to \infty$, every solution converges to $\mathbf{x}^*$ (global stability).

::: proof
Stability. Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be small enough that the closed ball $\bar B(\mathbf{x}^*, \varepsilon)$ lies in $U$, and $m = \min\{V(\mathbf{x}) : |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^*| = \varepsilon\} > 0$. By continuity, there exists $\delta < \varepsilon$ such that $V < m$ on $B(\mathbf{x}^*, \delta)$. A solution starting in this ball has $V(\mathbf{x}(t)) \le V(\mathbf{x}_0) < m$ for all $t$, since $V$ decreases; it can therefore never reach the sphere of radius $\varepsilon$.

Asymptotic stability. $V(\mathbf{x}(t))$ decreases and converges to a limit $c \ge 0$. If $c > 0$, the trajectory stays in the compact set $K = \{c \le V \le V(\mathbf{x}_0)\} \cap \bar B(\mathbf{x}^*, \varepsilon)$, which does not contain $\mathbf{x}^*$; $\dot V$ is bounded above there by some $-\kappa < 0$, whence $V(\mathbf{x}(t)) \le V(\mathbf{x}_0) - \kappa t$, which becomes negative: a contradiction. Hence $c = 0$, and $\mathbf{x}(t) \to \mathbf{x}^*$. The global case is handled in the same way, the sets $\{V \le c\}$ then being compact. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 2.10 — Gradient systems, the Lorenz system for $r < 1$]{.tag}
For a **gradient system** $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = -\nabla U(\mathbf{x})$, we have $\dot U = -|\nabla U|^2 \le 0$: the potential $U$ (up to a constant) is a Lyapunov function at each of its isolated strict minima. The double well of chapter 6 is of this type. For the Lorenz system with $r < 1$, the function $V = x^2/s + y^2 + z^2$ satisfies $\dot V = -2\big[(x - \tfrac{r+1}{2}y)^2 + (1 - \tfrac{(r+1)^2}{4})y^2\big] - 2bz^2 < 0$ away from the origin, which proves the **global** stability of $O$ (exercise 4).
:::

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 2
:::
- A fixed point is asymptotically stable if all the eigenvalues of the Jacobian have a negative real part, unstable if one is positive; the case of a zero real part is that of bifurcations.
- In dimension 2: saddle if $\det A < 0$; otherwise node or focus depending on the sign of $\tau^2 - 4\Delta$, stable if $\tau < 0$.
- A Lyapunov function ($V > 0$, $\dot V \le 0$) proves stability without solving the equation, sometimes globally.
- Lorenz: $O$ stable for $r < 1$, $C_\pm$ stable for $1 < r < r_H \approx 24.74$, all unstable at $r = 28$.
- Gissinger ($\mu = 0.119$, $\nu = 0.1$, $\Gamma = 0.9$): $O$ is a very weakly unstable focus ($0.0095 \pm 0.893\,i$), $N_\pm$ are unstable saddle-foci, $M_\pm$ do not exist.
::::

## 3. Local bifurcations and normal forms {#ch3}

When the magnetic Reynolds number of a dynamo experiment is increased, the state $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{0}$ loses its stability at a threshold $Rm_c$ and a field appears. Near the threshold, the amplitude of this field obeys a law that depends only on the **type** of bifurcation, not on the details of the flow. Normal forms are the simplest equations representing each type; every sufficiently regular system reduces to one of them near the threshold.

### 3.1 What is a bifurcation?

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Local bifurcation]{.tag}
Consider a family $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = F(\mathbf{x}, r)$ depending on a real parameter $r$. We say that $r_c$ is a **bifurcation value** if the phase portrait changes qualitatively when $r$ crosses $r_c$: number of fixed points or periodic orbits, or their stability. The bifurcation is **local** if it occurs in a neighborhood of a non-hyperbolic fixed point: $DF(\mathbf{x}^*, r_c)$ has a zero eigenvalue (stationary bifurcation) or a pair $\pm i\omega$ (Hopf bifurcation).
:::

::: note
[Remark 3.2 — Center manifold reduction]{.tag}
In a neighborhood of a non-hyperbolic fixed point, there exists an invariant manifold, the **center manifold**, tangent to the eigendirections of the eigenvalues with zero real part; the other directions relax exponentially toward it (theorem stated without proof; see Guckenheimer and Holmes, 1983, or Kuznetsov, 2023). The dynamics near the threshold therefore reduces to an equation of dimension 1 (zero eigenvalue) or 2 (imaginary pair), **whatever** the dimension $n$ of the original system, including for the discretized MHD equations. The normal forms below are these reduced equations, after a change of variables.
:::

### 3.2 The saddle-node

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.3 — Normal form of the saddle-node]{.tag}
For $\dot x = r + x^2$:

- if $r < 0$, there are two fixed points $x_\pm = \pm\sqrt{-r}$; $x_- = -\sqrt{-r}$ is stable and $x_+ = +\sqrt{-r}$ is unstable;
- if $r = 0$, they merge at $x = 0$, which is semi-stable;
- if $r > 0$, there is no fixed point anymore.

::: proof
The fixed points are the roots of $r + x^2 = 0$. Their stability is read off $f'(x) = 2x$: negative at $x_-$, positive at $x_+$ (theorem 2.4 in dimension 1). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Two fixed points, one stable and the other unstable, approach each other and then annihilate: this is the generic bifurcation in the absence of symmetry. Just past the threshold, a “ghost” remains: where the fixed point has disappeared, the velocity $\dot x = r + x^2$ remains very small, and the trajectory spends a long time there.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.4 — Bottleneck]{.tag}
For $r > 0$, the time taken to go from $x = -a$ to $x = +a$ is

$$
T(r) = \frac{2}{\sqrt r}\arctan\frac{a}{\sqrt r} = \frac{\pi}{\sqrt r} - \frac{2}{a} + O\big(r/a^3\big).
$$

The passage time diverges as $r^{-1/2}$ at the threshold.

::: proof
Since $\dot x > 0$, we change variables: $T = \int_{-a}^{a}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{r + x^2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt r}\Big[\arctan\frac{x}{\sqrt r}\Big]_{-a}^{a}$. The expansion $\arctan z = \pi/2 - 1/z + O(z^{-3})$ for $z = a/\sqrt r \to \infty$ gives the right-hand side. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 3.5 — Periodic reversals of Pétrélis and Fauve]{.tag}
Pétrélis and Fauve (2008) describe the field of a turbulent dynamo by a complex amplitude $A = D + iQ$ (dipole and quadrupole), whose phase obeys, after reduction,

$$
\dot\theta = \mu_i - \rho\sin 2\theta .
$$

For $|\mu_i| < \rho$, there are four fixed points, two of which are stable, $\theta_c$ and $\theta_c + \pi$: these are two dipoles of opposite polarities. At $\mu_i = \rho$, the fixed points disappear in pairs through a saddle-node; beyond it, $\theta$ rotates and the dipole $D \propto \cos(\theta + \theta_0)$ reverses periodically, with a time $\pi/\sqrt{\mu_i^2 - \rho^2}$ between two reversals (exercise 5). Near the threshold, this time diverges as $(\mu_i - \rho)^{-1/2}$, in agreement with proposition 3.4. Just below the threshold, it is the turbulent fluctuations that trigger random reversals (Pétrélis et al., 2009): this is the subject of chapter 6.
:::

### 3.3 The pitchfork

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.6 — Supercritical pitchfork]{.tag}
For $\dot x = rx - x^3$:

- if $r < 0$, only $x = 0$ is fixed, and it is stable;
- if $r > 0$, $x = 0$ is unstable and two stable fixed points $x_\pm = \pm\sqrt r$ appear.

The amplitude of the bifurcated state grows as $\sqrt r$, and the relaxation rate toward it is $2r$.

::: proof
The fixed points are $x = 0$ and $x^2 = r$. We have $f'(x) = r - 3x^2$, which equals $r$ at $0$ and $r - 3r = -2r$ at $\pm\sqrt r$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The relaxation rate $|r|$ or $2r$ tends to zero at the threshold: this is **critical slowing down**. An experiment or a simulation near a threshold therefore takes a very long time to reach its steady regime.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.7 — Subcritical pitchfork and hysteresis]{.tag}
For $\dot x = rx + x^3 - x^5$, the nonzero fixed points satisfy $x^2 = \big(1 \pm \sqrt{1 + 4r}\big)/2$. The “$+$” branch exists for $r \ge -1/4$ and is stable (for $r > -1/4$); the “$-$” branch exists for $-1/4 \le r < 0$ and is unstable; $x = 0$ is stable for $r < 0$. On the interval $\left]-1/4, 0\right[$, the zero state and the finite-amplitude state ($x^2 > 1/2$, i.e. $|x|$ between $0.71$ and $1$) are **both stable** (bistability).

::: proof
At a nonzero fixed point, $r + x^2 - x^4 = 0$, a quadratic equation in $x^2$ that gives the two branches. On these branches, $r = x^4 - x^2$, so $f'(x) = r + 3x^2 - 5x^4 = 2x^2 - 4x^4 = 2x^2(1 - 2x^2)$, which is negative if and only if $x^2 > 1/2$, that is, on the “$+$” branch. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

If $r$ is slowly increased from a negative value, the system stays at $x = 0$ until $r = 0$, then **jumps** to the finite-amplitude branch $|x| = 1$. On the way back down, it stays there until $r = -1/4$, where the stable branch disappears through a saddle-node, and it falls back to zero. The upward and downward paths differ: this is a **hysteresis** loop. A subcritical dynamo would thus appear abruptly, with a finite-amplitude field, and would persist below its onset threshold.

### 3.4 The Hopf bifurcation

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.8 — Hopf normal form]{.tag}
For the complex variable $z$ and

$$
\dot z = (\mu + i\omega)\,z - (1 + i\beta)\,|z|^2 z
$$

(here $\mu$ is the bifurcation parameter, unrelated to the coefficient $\mu$ of the Gissinger model),
the polar form $z = \varrho\,e^{i\theta}$ gives $\dot\varrho = \mu\varrho - \varrho^3$ and $\dot\theta = \omega - \beta\varrho^2$. For $\mu > 0$, there exists a stable **limit cycle** of radius $\sqrt\mu$ and period $2\pi/(\omega - \beta\mu)$.

::: proof
We compute $\dot z = (\dot\varrho + i\varrho\dot\theta)\,e^{i\theta}$ and identify with $\big[(\mu + i\omega)\varrho - (1 + i\beta)\varrho^3\big]e^{i\theta}$: real part $\dot\varrho = \mu\varrho - \varrho^3$, imaginary part $\varrho\dot\theta = \omega\varrho - \beta\varrho^3$. The radial equation is a supercritical pitchfork (proposition 3.6): $\varrho = \sqrt\mu$ is stable, and on this circle $\dot\theta = \omega - \beta\mu$ is constant. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.9 — Hopf (statement)]{.tag}
If the Jacobian $DF(\mathbf{x}^*, r)$ has a pair of simple eigenvalues $\alpha(r) \pm i\omega(r)$ with $\alpha(r_c) = 0$, $\alpha'(r_c) \ne 0$ and $\omega(r_c) \ne 0$, all the other eigenvalues having a negative real part, then a periodic orbit with amplitude proportional to $\sqrt{|r - r_c|}$ is born at $r_c$. If a computable coefficient, the first Lyapunov coefficient, is nonzero, this orbit exists past the threshold and is stable (**supercritical** Hopf), or exists before the threshold and is unstable (**subcritical** Hopf), depending on its sign.

::: proof
Stated without proof; see Kuznetsov (2023). The proof reduces the system to the center manifold (of dimension 2) and then brings the reduced equation to the normal form 3.8 through polynomial changes of variables. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

In the Lorenz system, the points $C_\pm$ lose their stability at $r_H \approx 24.74$ through a subcritical Hopf bifurcation: no stable orbit takes over, which leaves room for chaos (Strogatz, 2018). In the Gissinger model, the point $O$ becomes an unstable focus through a Hopf bifurcation when $\mu$ exceeds $\nu$, if $\mu + \nu < 2\Gamma$ (Gissinger, 2012).

### 3.5 Bifurcation with symmetry: the states $\pm\mathbf{B}$

::: def
[Definition 3.10 — Equivariant system]{.tag}
Let $S$ be an orthogonal matrix such that $S^2 = I$. The vector field $F$ is **equivariant** under $S$ (or “$S$ is a symmetry of the system”) if $F(S\mathbf{x}) = S\,F(\mathbf{x})$ for all $\mathbf{x}$. In this case, $\Phi^t(S\mathbf{x}) = S\,\Phi^t(\mathbf{x})$: the image under $S$ of a solution is a solution (same uniqueness argument as in proposition 1.9).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.11 — Symmetry makes the pitchfork generic]{.tag}
Let $\dot x = f(x, r)$ in dimension 1 with $f(-x, r) = -f(x, r)$ (symmetry $x \mapsto -x$), $f$ smooth, $\partial_x f(0, r_c) = 0$, $\partial_r\partial_x f(0, r_c) \ne 0$ and $\partial_x^3 f(0, r_c) \ne 0$. Then, near $(0, r_c)$, the dynamics is that of a pitchfork (super- or subcritical depending on the sign of $\partial_x^3 f$), and not that of a saddle-node.

::: proof
An odd function has only odd powers in its expansion: $f(x, r) = a(r)\,x + c(r)\,x^3 + O(x^5)$, with $a(r_c) = 0$. The even terms, which would produce a saddle-node, are forbidden by the symmetry. We set $\tilde r = a(r) \approx a'(r_c)(r - r_c)$, which changes sign at $r_c$, and, since $c(r_c) \ne 0$, $y = \sqrt{|c(r)|}\,x$: the equation becomes $\dot y = \tilde r\,y \pm y^3$ up to higher-order terms, with the sign of $c(r_c)$, that is, that of $\partial_x^3 f(0, r_c)$ (“$-$”: supercritical, “$+$”: subcritical). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

This is the situation of the dynamo. The induction equation $\partial_t\mathbf{B} = \nabla\times(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{B}) + \eta\Delta\mathbf{B}$ is **linear** in $\mathbf{B}$, and the Lorentz force $(\nabla\times\mathbf{B})\times\mathbf{B}$ is **quadratic**; the MHD equations are therefore invariant under $(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{B}) \mapsto (\mathbf{u}, -\mathbf{B})$. Every dynamo state $\mathbf{B}$ has a twin $-\mathbf{B}$, with exactly the same flow, and the bifurcation from $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{0}$ (for a real eigenvalue) is a pitchfork: two symmetric branches $\pm\mathbf{B}$ appear together. It is this symmetry that gives meaning to the word “reversal”.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.12 — Amplitude law near the threshold]{.tag}
Suppose that, near the threshold, the amplitude $A$ of the unstable mode obeys the reduced equation $\dot A = \kappa\,(R - R_c)\,A - g\,A^3$ with $\kappa > 0$ and $g > 0$ (supercritical pitchfork). Then, for $R > R_c$, the saturated state satisfies

$$
|A| = \sqrt{\frac{\kappa\,(R - R_c)}{g}}, \qquad A^2 \propto R - R_c .
$$

::: proof
This is proposition 3.6 after the change of variables $r = \kappa(R - R_c)$ and $x = \sqrt{g}\,A$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For a dynamo, the magnetic energy, proportional to $A^2$, therefore grows **linearly** with the distance to threshold $Rm - Rm_c$. This law holds only near the threshold and for a supercritical bifurcation; far from the threshold, or for a turbulent flow, other scaling laws appear (see the module [MHD and the dynamo effect](../p3-mhd-dynamo/index.html)).

### 3.6 Imperfection: when the symmetry is slightly broken

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.13 — Imperfect pitchfork and cusp]{.tag}
For $\dot x = h + rx - x^3$ with $h \ne 0$, the equation has three fixed points (two stable, one unstable) if $27h^2 < 4r^3$, and only one (stable) if $27h^2 > 4r^3$. The boundary $27h^2 = 4r^3$ in the $(r, h)$ plane is a **cusp**; on it, two fixed points are born or disappear through a saddle-node.

::: proof
The number of real roots of the polynomial $h + rx - x^3$ changes when a root becomes double: $f(x) = 0$ and $f'(x) = r - 3x^2 = 0$. The second condition gives $r = 3x^2$, then the first $h = x^3 - rx = -2x^3$. Eliminating $x$: $4r^3 = 4\cdot 27\,x^6 = 27\,(2x^3)^2 = 27h^2$. For $r \le 0$, $f$ is strictly decreasing and has only one root; for $r > 0$ and $h = 0$, we recover the three roots of the pitchfork, and this number is preserved as long as the boundary is not crossed. Stabilities are read off the sign of $f'$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Physically, a small term $h$ that breaks the symmetry $x \mapsto -x$ (for example an external magnetic field, such as the Earth's field, in a dynamo experiment) **selects a polarity**: the branch favored by the sign of $h$ appears continuously, while the other appears only after the saddle-node $r = 3\,(|h|/2)^{2/3}$. With $h = 0.05$, this saddle-node is at $r \approx 0.26$ (figure below, panel d). In the Gissinger model, the symmetry $\mathbf{B} \mapsto -\mathbf{B}$ remains exact for every $\Gamma$; the forcing $\Gamma$ sustains a velocity mode that breaks **another** symmetry, that of the flow with respect to the equatorial plane, and it is this breaking that couples dipole and quadrupole (Gissinger, Dormy and Fauve, 2010; Gissinger, 2012).

![Bifurcation diagrams of the four normal forms of the chapter. Horizontal axis: parameter r; vertical axis: position of the fixed points x*. Solid lines: stable branches; dashes or dots: unstable branches. (a) Saddle-node: two branches that meet at r = 0. (b) Supercritical pitchfork: the state x = 0 becomes unstable and two branches ±√r appear. (c) Subcritical pitchfork: the arrows show the hysteresis loop, a jump to |x| = 1 at r = 0 and a return to 0 at r = −1/4. (d) Imperfect pitchfork with h = 0.05: the upper branch is continuous, the lower branch is born through a saddle-node near r = 0.26.](../../../prep/p4-systemes-dynamiques/figures/bifurcations-en.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Four bifurcation diagrams in a two-by-two grid. Top left, a sideways parabola whose lower half is a solid blue line and upper half orange dashes, meeting at r equal 0. Top right, a pitchfork: a blue horizontal axis for negative r, dashed orange for positive r, and two blue square-root branches. Bottom left, the subcritical pitchfork with S-shaped branches, and two vertical arrows indicating the jumps at r equal 0 and r equal minus 0.25. Bottom right, a continuous increasing blue curve and, from r equal 0.26, a blue branch and an orange branch born together below the axis."}

The following code checks three predictions of the chapter: the exponent $1/2$ of the pitchfork, the passage time $\pi/\sqrt r$ of the saddle-node, and the hysteresis of the subcritical pitchfork.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp, quad

def etat_final(f, x0, T=400.0):
    """Integrates dx/dt = f(x) up to T and returns x(T)."""
    sol = solve_ivp(lambda t, x: f(x), (0.0, T), [x0], rtol=1e-10, atol=1e-12)
    return sol.y[0, -1]

# 1) Supercritical pitchfork dx/dt = r x - x^3: amplitude ~ r^(1/2)
rs = np.array([1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2, 3e-2, 1e-1])
amp = np.array([etat_final(lambda x, r=r: r * x - x**3, 0.01, T=40.0 / r) for r in rs])
pente = np.polyfit(np.log(rs), np.log(amp), 1)[0]
print("pitchfork: amplitudes", np.round(amp, 4), f"; fitted exponent = {pente:.3f}")

# 2) Saddle-node dx/dt = r + x^2 just past the threshold: passage time from x = -10 to x = +10
for r in (1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-4):
    T = quad(lambda x: 1.0 / (r + x**2), -10, 10, points=[0.0], limit=200)[0]
    print(f"saddle-node: r = {r:.0e}, passage time = {T:9.2f} ; pi/sqrt(r) = {np.pi / np.sqrt(r):9.2f}")

# 3) Subcritical pitchfork dx/dt = r x + x^3 - x^5: hysteresis
#    slow sweep of r upward then downward, each time starting from the previous state
#    (1e-6 is added at each step: a small perturbation, like the noise of an experiment)
def suivre(rs, x):
    out = []
    for r in rs:
        x = etat_final(lambda y, r=r: r * y + y**3 - y**5, x + 1e-6, T=400.0)
        out.append(x)
    return np.array(out)

r_haut = np.arange(-0.375, 0.15, 0.05)
monte = suivre(r_haut, 1e-3)
descend = suivre(r_haut[::-1], monte[-1])[::-1]
for r, a, b in zip(r_haut, monte, descend):
    print(f"r = {r:+.3f} : upward branch x = {a:6.3f} ; downward branch x = {b:6.3f}")
# output:
# pitchfork: amplitudes [0.0316 0.0548 0.1    0.1732 0.3162] ; fitted exponent = 0.500
# saddle-node: r = 1e-02, passage time =     31.22 ; pi/sqrt(r) =     31.42
# saddle-node: r = 1e-03, passage time =     99.15 ; pi/sqrt(r) =     99.35
# saddle-node: r = 1e-04, passage time =    313.96 ; pi/sqrt(r) =    314.16
# r = -0.375 : upward branch x =  0.000 ; downward branch x =  0.000
# r = -0.325 : upward branch x =  0.000 ; downward branch x =  0.000
# r = -0.275 : upward branch x =  0.000 ; downward branch x =  0.000
# r = -0.225 : upward branch x =  0.000 ; downward branch x =  0.811
# r = -0.175 : upward branch x =  0.000 ; downward branch x =  0.880
# r = -0.125 : upward branch x =  0.000 ; downward branch x =  0.924
# r = -0.075 : upward branch x =  0.000 ; downward branch x =  0.958
# r = -0.025 : upward branch x =  0.000 ; downward branch x =  0.987
# r = +0.025 : upward branch x =  0.022 ; downward branch x =  1.012
# r = +0.075 : upward branch x =  1.034 ; downward branch x =  1.034
# r = +0.125 : upward branch x =  1.055 ; downward branch x =  1.055
```

The fit on a log-log scale recovers the exponent $0.500$. The passage times differ from $\pi/\sqrt r$ by exactly $2/a = 0.2$, as stated in proposition 3.4. The upward sweep stays at $x = 0$ until $r = +0.025$ (critical slowing down delays the departure: at $r = 0.025$, the perturbation has grown only by a factor $e^{10}$ in 400 time units), then jumps to the branch $|x| \approx 1$; the downward sweep stays there until $r = -0.225$ and falls back to zero before $r = -0.275$, on either side of the saddle-node $r = -1/4$. The downward branch follows the formula: for $r = -0.225$, $x^2 = (1 + \sqrt{0.1})/2$, i.e. $x = 0.811$.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 3
:::
- A local bifurcation occurs when an eigenvalue (or a pair) crosses the imaginary axis; the dynamics then reduces to an equation of dimension 1 or 2 (center manifold).
- Saddle-node $\dot x = r + x^2$: two fixed points annihilate; passage time $\pi/\sqrt r$ past the threshold.
- Pitchfork $\dot x = rx - x^3$: amplitude $\sqrt r$, critical slowing down; the subcritical version gives a finite-amplitude jump and hysteresis between $r = -1/4$ and $r = 0$.
- Supercritical Hopf: a stable limit cycle of amplitude $\sqrt{\mu}$ is born from a focus; in the subcritical case, the oscillation appears abruptly with a finite amplitude.
- The symmetry $\mathbf{B} \mapsto -\mathbf{B}$ of MHD forbids even terms: the pitchfork is generic, the states $\pm\mathbf{B}$ appear together, and $|\mathbf{B}|^2 \propto Rm - Rm_c$ near a supercritical threshold.
- A small symmetry breaking $h$ unfolds the pitchfork (cusp $27h^2 = 4r^3$) and selects a polarity.
::::

## 4. Chaos: Lorenz, Lyapunov exponents, crises {#ch4}

Beyond the successive thresholds, the dynamics can become chaotic: bounded, non-periodic, and sensitive to initial conditions. This is the case of the Gissinger model in the reversal regime. This chapter defines and measures this sensitivity, then describes the **crisis** that merges two symmetric attractors: this is the deterministic mechanism of the reversals of chapter 7.

### 4.1 The Lorenz system

The Lorenz system (example 1.3) is invariant under $S : (x, y, z) \mapsto (-x, -y, z)$, the same symmetry structure as $(Q, D, V) \mapsto (-Q, -D, V)$ for Gissinger. Its scenario illustrates the previous chapters: at $r = 1$, the origin becomes unstable through a **pitchfork** (a symmetric one!) that creates $C_\pm$; at $r_H \approx 24.74$, $C_\pm$ become unstable through a subcritical **Hopf** bifurcation; at $r = 28$, the dynamics is chaotic.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.1 — Trapping region]{.tag}
Let $W(x, y, z) = x^2 + y^2 + (z - r - s)^2$. Along the solutions of Lorenz,

$$
\dot W = -2s\,x^2 - 2y^2 - 2b\Big(z - \frac{r+s}{2}\Big)^2 + \frac{b\,(r+s)^2}{2}.
$$

Consequently, $\dot W < 0$ outside a bounded ellipsoid $\mathcal{E}$; all solutions enter a ball $\{W \le R^2\}$ containing $\mathcal{E}$ and never leave it. They are therefore defined for all $t \ge 0$ and bounded.

::: proof
We expand: $\dot W = 2x\,s(y - x) + 2y\,\big(x(r - z) - y\big) + 2(z - r - s)(xy - bz)$. The terms in $xy$ have coefficient $2s + 2r - 2(r + s) = 0$, those in $xyz$ cancel ($-2xyz + 2xyz$), and what remains is $-2sx^2 - 2y^2 - 2bz^2 + 2b(r + s)z$. We complete the square in $z$. The ellipsoid $\mathcal{E} = \{s x^2 + y^2 + b(z - \tfrac{r+s}{2})^2 \le b(r+s)^2/4\}$ is bounded; we choose $R$ such that $\{W \le R^2\}$ contains it. On the compact set $\{R^2 \le W \le W(\mathbf{x}_0)\}$, $\dot W$ is bounded above by a constant $-\kappa < 0$, so $W$ decreases at least linearly until it falls below $R^2$, and it can never rise above it again since $\dot W < 0$ on the sphere $\{W = R^2\}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Combined with the contraction of volumes ($\nabla\cdot F = -41/3$), this proposition shows that trajectories accumulate on a bounded set of zero volume.

### 4.2 Sensitivity to initial conditions and Lyapunov exponents

::: def
[Definition 4.2 — Maximal Lyapunov exponent]{.tag}
For an initial condition $\mathbf{x}_0$ and a vector $\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}$, we set

$$
\lambda_1 = \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{1}{t}\ln\frac{|D\Phi^t(\mathbf{x}_0)\,\mathbf{v}|}{|\mathbf{v}|},
$$

for a generic $\mathbf{v}$. A small perturbation grows on average as $e^{\lambda_1 t}$. A bounded, non-periodic attractor with $\lambda_1 > 0$ is called **chaotic**.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.3 — Oseledets (statement)]{.tag}
If $\mu$ is an ergodic invariant measure (chapter 5), for example with compact support (which guarantees the integrability condition of the theorem), then for $\mu$-almost every $\mathbf{x}_0$ there exist $n$ exponents $\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n$, independent of $\mathbf{x}_0$, such that the growth rates of $|D\Phi^t(\mathbf{x}_0)\mathbf{v}|$ take these values depending on the direction of $\mathbf{v}$. The volume of a $k$-dimensional parallelepiped grows as $e^{(\lambda_1 + \dots + \lambda_k)t}$.

::: proof
Stated without proof; see Eckmann and Ruelle (1985), who also present the computation algorithm. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.4 — Sum of the exponents, zero exponent]{.tag}
*(i)* $\lambda_1 + \dots + \lambda_n = \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac1t\int_0^t \nabla\cdot F(\mathbf{x}(\tau))\,\mathrm{d}\tau$. For Lorenz, this sum equals $-(s + 1 + b) = -41/3$.

*(ii)* If the trajectory is bounded and does not tend to a fixed point, one of the exponents is zero: that of the direction of the flow.

::: proof
*(i)* The sum of the $n$ exponents is the growth rate of the volume of an $n$-dimensional parallelepiped, that is, of $|\det D\Phi^t(\mathbf{x}_0)|$ (theorem 4.3), and Liouville's formula (1.1) gives $\frac1t\ln\det D\Phi^t = \frac1t\int_0^t\nabla\cdot F$. (ii) Differentiating $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}F(\mathbf{x}(t)) = DF(\mathbf{x}(t))\,\dot{\mathbf{x}} = DF(\mathbf{x}(t))\,F(\mathbf{x}(t))$, we see that $F(\mathbf{x}(t))$ is a solution of the variational equation: $F(\mathbf{x}(t)) = D\Phi^t(\mathbf{x}_0)\,F(\mathbf{x}_0)$. Along a bounded trajectory that does not tend to a fixed point, $|F(\mathbf{x}(t))|$ stays bounded and does not tend to $0$, so its exponential growth rate is zero. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key point — Predictability horizon]{.tag}
An initial error $\delta_0$ reaches the size $\Delta$ of the attractor after a time

$$
T_p \approx \frac{1}{\lambda_1}\ln\frac{\Delta}{\delta_0}.
$$

The horizon grows only **logarithmically** with the precision: dividing the initial error by $10^4$ gains only $\ln(10^4)/\lambda_1$, about ten time units for Lorenz. Beyond $T_p$, only the statistics of the regime, that is, the invariant measure, is predictable.
:::

::: def
[Definition 4.5 — Kaplan–Yorke dimension]{.tag}
Let $k$ be the largest integer such that $\lambda_1 + \dots + \lambda_k \ge 0$. The Kaplan–Yorke dimension is $D_{KY} = k + (\lambda_1 + \dots + \lambda_k)/|\lambda_{k+1}|$. It estimates the fractal dimension of the attractor from the exponents.
:::

The numerical computation follows Benettin et al. (1980). The simplest method evolves two nearby trajectories and regularly brings their separation back to its initial size, accumulating the logarithms of the amplification factors; the renormalization prevents the separation from saturating at the size of the attractor. To obtain the whole spectrum, we integrate the variational equation with $n$ vectors that are regularly re-orthonormalized by a QR decomposition: the logarithms of the diagonal entries of $R$ give the successive growth rates.

```python
import numpy as np

s, r, b = 10.0, 28.0, 8.0 / 3.0       # Prandtl number s, reduced Rayleigh number r, geometric factor b

def F(x):
    return np.array([s * (x[1] - x[0]), x[0] * (r - x[2]) - x[1], x[0] * x[1] - b * x[2]])

def DF(x):
    return np.array([[-s, s, 0.0], [r - x[2], -1.0, -x[0]], [x[1], x[0], -b]])

def rk4(f, x, dt):
    k1 = f(x); k2 = f(x + 0.5 * dt * k1); k3 = f(x + 0.5 * dt * k2); k4 = f(x + dt * k3)
    return x + dt / 6 * (k1 + 2 * k2 + 2 * k3 + k4)

dt = 0.01
x = np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0])
for _ in range(2000):                       # transient: we reach the attractor
    x = rk4(F, x, dt)

# Method 1 (Benettin): two trajectories, renormalized to distance d0 every 0.5 time unit
d0, somme, n_renorm = 1e-8, 0.0, 400
xa, xb = x.copy(), x + np.array([d0, 0.0, 0.0])
for _ in range(n_renorm):
    for _ in range(50):
        xa, xb = rk4(F, xa, dt), rk4(F, xb, dt)
    d = np.linalg.norm(xb - xa)
    somme += np.log(d / d0)
    xb = xa + (xb - xa) * (d0 / d)                # bring the separation back to d0 in the same direction
print(f"method 1: lambda_1 ≈ {somme / (n_renorm * 0.5):.3f}")

# Method 2: linearized equation dM/dt = DF(x) M and QR orthonormalization (full spectrum)
def G(y):
    x, M = y[:3], y[3:].reshape(3, 3)
    return np.concatenate([F(x), (DF(x) @ M).ravel()])

y = np.concatenate([x, np.eye(3).ravel()])
S, T = np.zeros(3), 0.0
for k in range(30000):                        # 300 time units
    y = rk4(G, y, dt)
    if k % 10 == 9:
        Q, R = np.linalg.qr(y[3:].reshape(3, 3))
        S += np.log(np.abs(np.diag(R)))
        y[3:] = Q.ravel()
        T += 10 * dt
lam = S / T
print("method 2: exponents =", ", ".join(f"{l:+.3f}" for l in lam))
print(f"sum = {lam.sum():.3f} ; div F = -(s + 1 + b) = {-(s + 1 + b):.3f}")
print(f"Kaplan-Yorke dimension = 2 + (l1 + l2)/|l3| = {2 + (lam[0] + lam[1]) / abs(lam[2]):.3f}")
print(f"predictability horizon from 1e-8 to 1: ln(1e8)/lambda_1 = {np.log(1e8) / lam[0]:.1f}")
# output:
# method 1: lambda_1 ≈ 0.901
# method 2: exponents = +0.898, -0.003, -14.561
# sum = -13.667 ; div F = -(s + 1 + b) = -13.667
# Kaplan-Yorke dimension = 2 + (l1 + l2)/|l3| = 2.061
# predictability horizon from 1e-8 to 1: ln(1e8)/lambda_1 = 20.5
```

Both methods give $\lambda_1 \approx 0.90$. The second exponent is zero to within $3\times 10^{-3}$ (proposition 4.4 (ii)), and the sum of the three recovers exactly the divergence $-41/3$, which validates the computation. The dimension $D_{KY} \approx 2.06$ says that the attractor is “a little more than a surface”: a lamination of infinitely many sheets. The predictability horizon is about 20 time units to go from $10^{-8}$ to $1$. In chapter 1, the separation only reached $0.2$ around $t = 30$: the initial condition $(1, 1, 1)$ was not yet on the attractor and the perturbation was not aligned with the most unstable direction, so that exponential growth at rate $\lambda_1$ only set in after a transient (between $t = 20$ and $t = 30$, the separation is indeed multiplied by about $e^{10}$). The order of magnitude is the same.

![The Lorenz system for s = 10, b = 8/3, r = 28. (a) Projection of the attractor onto the (x, z) plane: two wings centered on C+ and C−, visited alternately. (b) Distance between two trajectories initially separated by 10⁻⁸, on a logarithmic scale: exponential growth with mean slope λ₁ ≈ 0.90 (dashes) until saturation at the size of the attractor around t ≈ 25.](../../../prep/p4-systemes-dynamiques/figures/lorenz-en.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Two panels. On the left, the butterfly-shaped curve of the Lorenz attractor in the plane with x horizontal and z vertical, with two loops around x equal minus 8 and plus 8, z between 5 and 45. On the right, on a logarithmic scale, the distance between two trajectories, which starts at 1e-8 at t equal 0, grows while oscillating around a dashed line of slope 0.90, then saturates around 10 from t equal 25."}

### 4.3 Strange attractors

::: def
[Definition 4.6 — Attractor, basin, strange attractor]{.tag}
An **attractor** is a compact invariant set $\mathcal{A}$ that attracts all trajectories starting in an open neighborhood, and that contains a dense orbit (it does not decompose into several smaller attractors). Its **basin** is the set of initial conditions whose trajectory converges to $\mathcal{A}$. An attractor is called **strange** if it has a fractal structure and if the dynamics on it is sensitive to initial conditions.
:::

Ruelle and Takens (1971) proposed that the onset of turbulence goes through such attractors, rather than through the accumulation of a large number of frequencies. The existence of the Lorenz attractor for the classical parameters, long observed numerically, was only proved in 1999, by a computer-assisted proof (Tucker, 1999).

### 4.4 Crises and merging of two symmetric attractors

::: def
[Definition 4.7 — Crisis]{.tag}
A **crisis** (Grebogi, Ott and Yorke, 1982) is a sudden change of a chaotic attractor when a parameter $p$ crosses a value $p_c$, caused by the collision of the attractor with an unstable periodic orbit or with the boundary of its basin. One distinguishes the boundary crisis (the attractor disappears and leaves behind transient chaos), the interior crisis (the attractor suddenly grows) and the **merging crisis**: two attractors simultaneously touch the boundary separating their basins and merge into one.
:::

In a system equivariant under $S$, the image $S(\mathcal{A})$ of an attractor is again an attractor, with basin $S(\text{basin})$. Generically, two situations arise: either $\mathcal{A} = S(\mathcal{A})$ is a **symmetric** attractor, or $\mathcal{A}$ and $S(\mathcal{A})$ form a **pair** of disjoint attractors. The transition from the second situation to the first, as a parameter varies, is typically a merging crisis.

::: ex
[Example 4.8 — The scenario of chaotic reversals]{.tag}
Before the crisis, there are two chaotic attractors $\mathcal{A}_+$ (dipole $D > 0$) and $\mathcal{A}_- = S(\mathcal{A}_+)$ ($D < 0$): a trajectory stays on one side forever, and the field never reverses. Just after the crisis, the two attractors have become connected by a narrow “corridor”: a trajectory spends long periods near the former $\mathcal{A}_+$, then switches to near the former $\mathcal{A}_-$, and so on. This regime of **crisis-induced intermittency** produces irregular reversals without any external noise. The mean duration $\tau$ between two switches diverges at the threshold as a power law $\tau \propto |p - p_c|^{-\gamma}$, with a critical exponent $\gamma$ specific to the system (Grebogi, Ott, Romeiras and Yorke, 1987). For the Gissinger model, at $\Gamma = 0.9$ and $\nu = 0.1$, the crisis occurs at $\mu_c \approx 0.11928$, and the author estimates $\gamma \simeq 1/2$, stressing that the conclusion is delicate because it is very sensitive to the value of $\mu_c$ (Gissinger, 2012). In this repository, with $\mu = 0.119$ fixed and $\Gamma$ varied, the crisis is observed between $\Gamma = 0.86$ and $0.87$ (chapter 7).
:::

For Lorenz at $r = 28$, the merging has already taken place: the attractor is symmetric, and the passage from one wing to the other (from $x > 0$ to $x < 0$) plays the role of a reversal.
