Key takeaways — chapter 4
:::
- Lorenz: all solutions enter a bounded trapping region, and volumes contract as $e^{-41t/3}$; the attractor has zero volume.
- The Lyapunov exponent $\lambda_1 \approx 0.90$ (Lorenz) measures the mean amplification of errors; the sum of the exponents equals the mean divergence; one exponent is zero (direction of the flow).
- Predictability horizon $T_p \approx \lambda_1^{-1}\ln(\Delta/\delta_0)$: beyond it, only the invariant measure is predictable.
- Benettin's algorithm: renormalization of the separation, or variational equation with QR orthonormalization.
- A merging crisis connects two symmetric attractors $\mathcal{A}_\pm$: the result is chaotic reversals, with a mean time between switches that diverges at the threshold as a power law.
::::

## 5. Invariant measures, Liouville and Fokker–Planck {#ch5}

The Lyapunov exponent makes the prediction of a trajectory impossible beyond a few characteristic times. Yet the mean, the histogram or the spectrum of a long simulation are reproducible from one initial condition to another. The stable object, the one that the generative models of the internship seek to learn, is the **invariant measure** $\mu_{\boldsymbol\lambda}$: the distribution of the state in the steady regime, for given parameters $\boldsymbol\lambda$. This chapter defines it, establishes its equations (Liouville without noise, Fokker–Planck with noise), and proves the stationarity identities that serve as constraints “in distribution” in the internship.

In this chapter, $\mu$ denotes a measure. When the Gissinger model comes in, its parameter $\mu = 0.119$ appears only as a numerical coefficient, and its distributions are denoted $\mu_\Gamma$, $\mu^\pm_\Gamma$.

### 5.1 Invariant measures

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Invariant measure]{.tag}
A probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is **invariant** under the flow if $\mu\big((\Phi^t)^{-1}(A)\big) = \mu(A)$ for every measurable set $A$ and every $t \ge 0$. Equivalently, $\mathbb{E}_\mu[g\circ\Phi^t] = \mathbb{E}_\mu[g]$ for every bounded continuous function $g$. In other words: if the initial condition $X_0$ has distribution $\mu$, then $X_t = \Phi^t(X_0)$ still has distribution $\mu$ at every instant (stationarity in distribution).
:::

::: ex
[Example 5.2 — Three invariant measures]{.tag}
*(a)* The Dirac mass $\delta_{\mathbf{x}^*}$ at a fixed point. (b) For a periodic orbit $\mathbf{x}(t)$ of period $T$, the measure $\frac1T\int_0^T\delta_{\mathbf{x}(t)}\,\mathrm{d}t$, which weights each arc in proportion to the time spent on it: its density along the curve is proportional to $1/|F|$. (c) For Lorenz, the **natural measure**, the limit of the histogram of a long typical trajectory.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.3 — Krylov–Bogoliubov]{.tag}
If the flow leaves a compact set $K$ invariant (for example a trapping region), there exists at least one invariant probability measure supported on $K$.

::: proof
Sketch. For $\mathbf{x}_0 \in K$, consider the empirical measures $\mu_T = \frac1T\int_0^T\delta_{\Phi^t(\mathbf{x}_0)}\,\mathrm{d}t$, that is, $\mathbb{E}_{\mu_T}[g] = \frac1T\int_0^T g(\Phi^t(\mathbf{x}_0))\,\mathrm{d}t$. These are probability measures on the compact set $K$; one can extract from them a sequence $\mu_{T_k}$ that converges weakly to a probability measure $\mu$ (Prokhorov's theorem). For $g$ bounded continuous and $s > 0$ fixed,

$$
\big|\mathbb{E}_{\mu_T}[g\circ\Phi^s] - \mathbb{E}_{\mu_T}[g]\big| = \frac1T\Big|\int_T^{T+s} g(\Phi^t\mathbf{x}_0)\,\mathrm{d}t - \int_0^s g(\Phi^t\mathbf{x}_0)\,\mathrm{d}t\Big| \le \frac{2s\,\sup|g|}{T},
$$

which tends to $0$. Passing to the limit along $T_k$, we obtain $\mathbb{E}_\mu[g\circ\Phi^s] = \mathbb{E}_\mu[g]$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

There are in general **many** invariant measures. For Lorenz at $r = 28$: the Dirac masses at $O$, $C_+$ and $C_-$, the measures supported by each of the infinitely many unstable periodic orbits of the attractor, the natural measure, and all their convex combinations. The question “which one is the right one?” is the subject of sections 5.2 and 5.6.

### 5.2 Ergodicity, Birkhoff's theorem, physical measure

::: def
[Definition 5.4 — Ergodicity]{.tag}
A set $A$ is **invariant** if $(\Phi^t)^{-1}(A) = A$ for all $t$. An invariant measure $\mu$ is **ergodic** if every invariant set has measure $\mu(A)$ equal to $0$ or $1$: the support of $\mu$ cannot be split into two invariant pieces that each have positive mass.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.5 — Birkhoff's ergodic theorem (statement)]{.tag}
Let $\mu$ be invariant and $g$ integrable with respect to $\mu$. For $\mu$-almost every initial condition, the time average $\bar g(\mathbf{x}_0) = \lim_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\int_0^T g(\Phi^t(\mathbf{x}_0))\,\mathrm{d}t$ exists. If $\mu$ is ergodic, it equals the ensemble average:

$$
\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\int_0^T g(\Phi^t(\mathbf{x}_0))\,\mathrm{d}t = \mathbb{E}_\mu[g] \quad\text{for } \mu\text{-almost every } \mathbf{x}_0 .
$$

::: proof
Stated without proof (Birkhoff, 1931). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

This theorem justifies the practice of the whole internship: a stationary distribution is estimated by sampling **one long trajectory** (or a few). But the statement contains a trap: “for $\mu$-almost every $\mathbf{x}_0$”. If $\mu$ is supported by an attractor of zero volume, this set of initial conditions itself has zero volume, and the theorem says nothing about initial conditions drawn at random with a density, as in a simulation.

::: def
[Definition 5.6 — Physical measure, SRB measure (statement)]{.tag}
An invariant measure $\mu$ is **physical** if the set of $\mathbf{x}_0$ for which $\frac1T\int_0^T g(\Phi^t\mathbf{x}_0)\,\mathrm{d}t \to \mathbb{E}_\mu[g]$ for every continuous $g$ has strictly positive **volume** (Lebesgue measure); this set is its basin. Sinai–Ruelle–Bowen (SRB) measures are invariant measures whose conditional measures along the unstable manifolds have a density. According to Young (2002): for uniformly hyperbolic attractors (Axiom A), an SRB measure exists, it is physical, and it is the limit, as the noise tends to zero, of the stationary distributions of the noisy system; it is, however, **singular** with respect to volume in the stable directions, since the support of an attractor that contracts volumes has zero volume.
:::

For the Lorenz and Gissinger systems, we assume the existence of one physical measure per attractor, and we observe it numerically: the histograms of different trajectories converge to the same limit. The practical consequence is important: **the stationary distribution has no density** on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Any equation that characterizes it must therefore be written in weak form, with test functions.

### 5.3 The Liouville equation

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.7 — Transport of densities]{.tag}
If $X_0$ has a smooth density $\rho_0$ and $X_t = \Phi^t(X_0)$, then the density $\rho(\mathbf{x}, t)$ of $X_t$ satisfies the **Liouville equation** (or continuity equation)

$$
\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} + \nabla\cdot(\rho\,F) = 0 .
$$

::: proof
Let $\varphi$ be a smooth compactly supported test function. By the chain rule, $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\varphi(X_t) = \nabla\varphi(X_t)\cdot F(X_t)$, so

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int\varphi\,\rho\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x} = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_t)] = \int \rho\,F\cdot\nabla\varphi\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x} = -\int\varphi\,\nabla\cdot(\rho F)\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x},
$$

the last equality being an integration by parts without boundary terms ($\varphi$ has compact support). The left-hand side equals $\int\varphi\,\partial_t\rho\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}$. Since the equality holds for every $\varphi$, $\partial_t\rho = -\nabla\cdot(\rho F)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Expanding, $\partial_t\rho + F\cdot\nabla\rho = -\rho\,\nabla\cdot F$: along a trajectory, the density **increases** where volumes contract. For Lorenz, it is multiplied by $e^{41t/3}$: it cannot converge to any function, and the limiting distribution is singular. The same continuity equation governs the transport of a distribution by the velocity field $v_\theta$ of a flow matching model (module [Generative models](../p7-modeles-generatifs/index.html)); the difference is that, there, one wants to transport noise to the data in finite time, whereas here one is looking for a distribution that no longer moves.

A stationary density, if it exists, satisfies $\nabla\cdot(\rho F) = 0$.

### 5.4 With noise: the Fokker–Planck equation

Reduced dynamo models (Pétrélis et al., 2009) often represent the effect of the small turbulent scales by a noise. We consider the stochastic differential equation

$$
\mathrm{d}X_t = F(X_t)\,\mathrm{d}t + \sigma\,\mathrm{d}W_t ,
$$

where $W$ is a Brownian motion in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\sigma > 0$ the noise amplitude. Numerically, it is integrated with the **Euler–Maruyama** scheme: $X_{k+1} = X_k + F(X_k)\,\Delta t + \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\,\boldsymbol\xi_k$, with independent standard Gaussian $\boldsymbol\xi_k$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.8 — Generator]{.tag}
For smooth $\varphi$, $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_t)] = \mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}\varphi(X_t)]$, where the **generator** is

$$
\mathcal{L}\varphi = F\cdot\nabla\varphi + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\,\Delta\varphi .
$$

::: proof
Heuristic proof on one Euler–Maruyama step. A second-order Taylor expansion gives

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\varphi(\mathbf{x} + F\Delta t + \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\,\boldsymbol\xi)\big] = \varphi(\mathbf{x}) + \Delta t\,F\cdot\nabla\varphi + \frac{\sigma^2\Delta t}{2}\,\mathbb{E}\big[\boldsymbol\xi^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2\varphi\,\boldsymbol\xi\big] + o(\Delta t),
$$

since $\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol\xi] = \mathbf{0}$ and the terms in $\Delta t^{3/2}$ and higher are negligible. Since $\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol\xi\boldsymbol\xi^{\mathsf T}] = I$, we have $\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol\xi^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2\varphi\,\boldsymbol\xi] = \operatorname{tr}\nabla^2\varphi = \Delta\varphi$. We divide by $\Delta t$ and let $\Delta t$ tend to $0$. The term in $\sigma^2$ comes from the fact that the Brownian increment is of order $\sqrt{\Delta t}$ and not $\Delta t$: this is the content of Itô's formula. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.9 — Fokker–Planck equation]{.tag}
If $X_t$ has a smooth density $\rho(\mathbf{x}, t)$, then

$$
\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} = -\nabla\cdot(\rho\,F) + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\,\Delta\rho .
$$

::: proof
By proposition 5.8, $\int\varphi\,\partial_t\rho = \int\rho\,\big(F\cdot\nabla\varphi + \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}\Delta\varphi\big)$. One integration by parts on the first term and two on the second give $\int\varphi\,\big(-\nabla\cdot(\rho F) + \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}\Delta\rho\big)$. We conclude as for proposition 5.7. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The noise adds a diffusion term that smooths the density: with $\sigma > 0$, the stationary distribution generally has a smooth density, unlike the deterministic case.

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.10 — Stationary density of a gradient system in dimension 1]{.tag}
For $\mathrm{d}X = -U'(X)\,\mathrm{d}t + \sigma\,\mathrm{d}W$ on $\mathbb{R}$, with $e^{-2U/\sigma^2}$ integrable, the stationary density is

$$
\rho(x) = \frac{1}{Z}\exp\Big(-\frac{2\,U(x)}{\sigma^2}\Big), \qquad Z = \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-2U/\sigma^2}\,\mathrm{d}x .
$$

::: proof
In dimension 1, the stationary equation reads $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}J = 0$ with the flux $J = -U'\rho - \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\rho'$, which can be rewritten $J = -\frac{\sigma^2}{2}\,e^{-2U/\sigma^2}\,h'$ with $h = \rho\,e^{2U/\sigma^2} \ge 0$. The flux is therefore a constant $J$. Let us show that it is zero. If $J > 0$, then $h' = -\frac{2J}{\sigma^2}e^{2U/\sigma^2}$ and $h(x) = h(0) - \frac{2J}{\sigma^2}\int_0^x e^{2U/\sigma^2}$; now, by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, $x^2 = \big(\int_0^x e^{U/\sigma^2}e^{-U/\sigma^2}\big)^2 \le Z\int_0^x e^{2U/\sigma^2}$, so this integral tends to $+\infty$ and $h$ would become negative for large $x$: this is impossible. The case $J < 0$ is handled in the same way at $-\infty$. Hence $J = 0$, $h$ is constant, and $\rho \propto e^{-2U/\sigma^2}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

This is the Boltzmann distribution, with $\sigma^2/2$ playing the role of temperature: the noise plays the role of thermal agitation. For a symmetric potential, this density is symmetric; we will use this in section 5.6.

### 5.5 Stationary weak form: the stationarity identities

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.11 — Stationarity identities]{.tag}
Let $\mu$ be an invariant measure of the deterministic system ($\sigma = 0$), or a stationary distribution of the noisy system ($\sigma > 0$). For every test function $\varphi$ of class $C^2$ with compact support (or polynomial, if $\mu$ has enough moments for the expectations to make sense),

$$
\mathbb{E}_\mu\Big[F\cdot\nabla\varphi + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\,\Delta\varphi\Big] = \mathbb{E}_\mu[\mathcal{L}\varphi] = 0 . \tag{5.1}
$$

::: proof
*First proof (through the distribution).* If $X_0 \sim \mu$, then $X_t \sim \mu$ for all $t$, so $\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_t)]$ does not depend on $t$. By proposition 5.8 (or by the simple chain rule if $\sigma = 0$), $0 = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_t)]\big|_{t=0} = \mathbb{E}_\mu[\mathcal{L}\varphi]$.

*Second proof (through time averages, without a density).* Take first $\sigma = 0$ and a bounded trajectory. By the chain rule, $\varphi(\mathbf{x}(T)) - \varphi(\mathbf{x}(0)) = \int_0^T F\cdot\nabla\varphi(\mathbf{x}(t))\,\mathrm{d}t$. Divide by $T$: the left-hand side is bounded by $2\sup_K|\varphi|/T$, where $K$ is a compact set containing the trajectory, and tends to $0$. The right-hand side is a time average, which converges to $\mathbb{E}_\mu[F\cdot\nabla\varphi]$ for a typical initial condition of a physical measure (or of an ergodic one, by Birkhoff's theorem). Hence $\mathbb{E}_\mu[F\cdot\nabla\varphi] = 0$. With $\sigma > 0$, Itô's formula adds to the right-hand side the term $\int_0^T\frac{\sigma^2}{2}\Delta\varphi\,\mathrm{d}t$ and a stochastic integral $M_T = \sigma\int_0^T\nabla\varphi\cdot\mathrm{d}W_t$, centered and with variance at most $\sigma^2 T\sup|\nabla\varphi|^2$; so $M_T/T$ has a variance of order $1/T$ and tends to $0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The second proof is the one that matters for turbulence and the dynamo: it uses neither a density nor the Liouville equation in the strong sense, only a bounded trajectory and the convergence of time averages. It also shows that the error of a **time** average on $\mathbb{E}_\mu[F\cdot\nabla\varphi]$ is a telescoping term of order $1/T$, much smaller than the statistical error of an independent sample of the same size.

::: note
[Remark 5.12 — The converse]{.tag}
For a Markov process, the condition $\mathbb{E}_\mu[\mathcal{L}\varphi] = 0$ for every $\varphi$ in a sufficiently rich class is necessary; its sufficiency requires additional assumptions (Echeverría's criterion, 1982; see also Ethier and Kurtz, 1986). For a non-degenerate diffusion ($\sigma > 0$) with a smooth, confining drift, the stationary distribution is moreover unique (Pavliotis, 2014). Without noise, on the other hand, the identities (5.1) are satisfied by **all** invariant measures, including the Dirac masses at the fixed points: on their own, they do not characterize the physical measure (section 5.6).
:::

::: key
[Key point — One test function, one constraint in distribution]{.tag}
Each test function $\varphi$ provides a linear identity $\mathbb{E}_\mu[F\cdot\nabla\varphi + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\Delta\varphi] = 0$ that every stationary distribution must satisfy. It does not bear on an isolated sample but on the **distribution**; it can be checked on generated samples, without knowing their temporal order or their density.
:::

::: ex
[Example 5.13 — The energy budget is the case $\varphi$ = energy]{.tag}
For the Gissinger model and $\varphi = E = (Q^2 + D^2 + V^2)/2$, we compute $F\cdot\nabla E = Q(\mu Q - VD) + D(-\nu D + VQ) + V(\Gamma - V + QD) = \mu Q^2 - \nu D^2 + \Gamma V - V^2 + QDV$. The identity (5.1) becomes

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\mu_\Gamma}\big[\mu Q^2 - \nu D^2 + \Gamma V - V^2 + QDV\big] = 0 :
$$

on average, the injected power balances the dissipated power, even if $\mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}t$ fluctuates at every instant. For the incompressible MHD equations forced in a periodic box, with $\varphi = E = \frac12\langle|\mathbf{u}|^2 + |\mathbf{B}|^2\rangle$ (notation shared by all the modules), we have $F\cdot\nabla E = \mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}t = \langle\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{f}\rangle - \nu\langle|\boldsymbol\omega|^2\rangle - \eta\langle|\mathbf{j}|^2\rangle$ (the nonlinear terms cancel; see the module [MHD and the dynamo effect](../p3-mhd-dynamo/index.html)). The stationary identity is then “mean injection = mean dissipation”, $\mathbb{E}_\mu[\langle\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{f}\rangle] = \mathbb{E}_\mu[\nu\langle|\boldsymbol\omega|^2\rangle + \eta\langle|\mathbf{j}|^2\rangle]$: this is the constraint “in distribution” of the energy budget of experiment E2 (see the [report](../../rapport/index.html#e2)). With a white-in-time random forcing, the term $\frac{\sigma^2}{2}\Delta E$ adds the rate of energy injection by the noise.
:::

For Lorenz, the simplest test functions give explicit identities: $\varphi = x$ gives $\mathbb{E}[x] = \mathbb{E}[y]$; $\varphi = z$ gives $\mathbb{E}[xy] = b\,\mathbb{E}[z]$; $\varphi = x^2/2$ gives $\mathbb{E}[x^2] = \mathbb{E}[xy]$; $\varphi = z^2/2$ gives $\mathbb{E}[xyz] = b\,\mathbb{E}[z^2]$. For Gissinger, $\varphi = Q^2/2$ and $\varphi = D^2/2$ give $\mu\,\mathbb{E}[Q^2] = \mathbb{E}[QDV] = \nu\,\mathbb{E}[D^2]$, and $\varphi = V$ gives $\mathbb{E}[V] = \Gamma + \mathbb{E}[QD]$ (exercises 8 and 9). The following code checks these identities on simulations; the “residual” is $|\text{mean}|/\text{standard deviation}$ of the quantity $F\cdot\nabla\varphi$, which is zero for an exactly stationary distribution.

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def rk4(f, X, dt):
    k1 = f(X); k2 = f(X + 0.5 * dt * k1); k3 = f(X + 0.5 * dt * k2); k4 = f(X + dt * k3)
    return X + dt / 6 * (k1 + 2 * k2 + 2 * k3 + k4)

def echantillonner(f, X, dt, t_transitoire, t_garde, tous_les):
    """N trajectories in parallel (X of shape (3, N)); returns the states (n_times, 3, N)."""
    for _ in range(int(t_transitoire / dt)):
        X = rk4(f, X, dt)
    out = []
    for k in range(int(t_garde / dt)):
        X = rk4(f, X, dt)
        if k % int(tous_les / dt) == 0:
            out.append(X.copy())
    return np.array(out)

def residu(g):
    """|mean| / standard deviation of the quantity g = F.grad(phi) evaluated on the sample."""
    return abs(g.mean()) / g.std()

# --- Lorenz (s, r, b) = (10, 28, 8/3) ---
s, r, b = 10.0, 28.0, 8.0 / 3.0
lorenz = lambda X: np.array([s * (X[1] - X[0]), X[0] * (r - X[2]) - X[1], X[0] * X[1] - b * X[2]])
E = echantillonner(lorenz, rng.normal(size=(3, 50)) * 5 + np.array([[0], [0], [25]]), 0.005, 20, 200, 0.05)
x, y, z = E[:, 0].ravel(), E[:, 1].ravel(), E[:, 2].ravel()
print(f"Lorenz, {x.size} samples:")
tests = {"phi = x      : s (y - x)": s * (y - x),
         "phi = z      : xy - b z": x * y - b * z,
         "phi = x^2/2  : s x (y - x)": s * x * (y - x),
         "phi = z^2/2  : xyz - b z^2": x * y * z - b * z**2}
for nom, g in tests.items():
    print(f"  {nom:32s} residual = {residu(g):.4f}")
print(f"  E[x^2] = {np.mean(x*x):.2f}, E[xy] = {np.mean(x*y):.2f}, b E[z] = {b*np.mean(z):.2f}")

# --- Gissinger (mu, nu) = (0.119, 0.1) ---
mu, nu = 0.119, 0.1
def gissinger(G):
    return lambda X: np.array([mu * X[0] - X[2] * X[1], -nu * X[1] + X[2] * X[0], G - X[2] + X[0] * X[1]])

for G in (0.90, 0.84):
    X0 = rng.normal(size=(3, 40)) * 0.8; X0[2] = np.abs(X0[2])
    E = echantillonner(gissinger(G), X0, 0.02, 400, 1500, 0.5)       # (n, 3, 40)
    q, d, v = E[:, 0], E[:, 1], E[:, 2]
    print(f"Gissinger, Gamma = {G} : mu E[Q^2] = {mu*np.mean(q*q):.4f}, nu E[D^2] = {nu*np.mean(d*d):.4f} ;"
          f" E[V] = {np.mean(v):.4f}, Gamma + E[QD] = {G + np.mean(q*d):.4f}")
    if G == 0.84:
        # Below the threshold: each trajectory stays on one of the two symmetric attractors.
        plus = d.mean(0) > 0
        print(f"  trajectories on the attractor D > 0: {plus.sum()} / {plus.size}")
        lp = E[:, :, plus].transpose(0, 2, 1).reshape(-1, 3)
        lm = E[:, :, ~plus].transpose(0, 2, 1).reshape(-1, 3)
        if lm.shape[0] == 0:                       # image under the symmetry if no trajectory is there
            lm = lp * np.array([-1, -1, 1])
        for p in (1.0, 0.75, 0.5, 0.0):            # mixture p mu+ + (1 - p) mu-
            n = 20000
            k = rng.binomial(n, p)
            S = np.vstack([lp[rng.integers(len(lp), size=k)], lm[rng.integers(len(lm), size=n - k)]])
            Q, D, V = S.T
            phis = [mu*Q - V*D, -nu*D + V*Q, G - V + Q*D,             # phi = Q, D, V
                    mu*Q*Q - Q*V*D, -nu*D*D + V*Q*D,                  # phi = Q^2/2, D^2/2
                    mu*Q*Q - nu*D*D + G*V - V*V + Q*D*V]              # phi = energy
            print(f"  p = {p:4.2f} : E[D] = {D.mean():+.3f} ; max of the 6 residuals = {max(residu(g) for g in phis):.4f}")
# output:
# Lorenz, 200000 samples:
#   phi = x      : s (y - x)         residual = 0.0002
#   phi = z      : xy - b z          residual = 0.0002
#   phi = x^2/2  : s x (y - x)       residual = 0.0001
#   phi = z^2/2  : xyz - b z^2       residual = 0.0001
#   E[x^2] = 62.83, E[xy] = 62.83, b E[z] = 62.82
# Gissinger, Gamma = 0.9 : mu E[Q^2] = 0.1362, nu E[D^2] = 0.1362 ; E[V] = -0.0788, Gamma + E[QD] = -0.0789
# Gissinger, Gamma = 0.84 : mu E[Q^2] = 0.1235, nu E[D^2] = 0.1235 ; E[V] = -0.0935, Gamma + E[QD] = -0.0935
#   trajectories on the attractor D > 0: 15 / 40
#   p = 1.00 : E[D] = +1.072 ; max of the 6 residuals = 0.0140
#   p = 0.75 : E[D] = +0.537 ; max of the 6 residuals = 0.0059
#   p = 0.50 : E[D] = +0.006 ; max of the 6 residuals = 0.0105
#   p = 0.00 : E[D] = -1.068 ; max of the 6 residuals = 0.0093
```

For Lorenz, the residuals are of order $10^{-4}$: these are time averages, whose error is the telescoping term of the second proof. The identities between moments are satisfied to three or four digits. For Gissinger, $\mu\,\mathbb{E}[Q^2] = \nu\,\mathbb{E}[D^2]$ and $\mathbb{E}[V] = \Gamma + \mathbb{E}[QD]$ are satisfied at both values of $\Gamma$. The last part of the code is explained in the next section.

### 5.6 The convex set of invariant measures

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.14 — Convexity]{.tag}
The set $\mathcal{M}$ of invariant probability measures is convex: if $\mu_1, \mu_2 \in \mathcal{M}$ and $p \in [0, 1]$, then $p\,\mu_1 + (1 - p)\,\mu_2 \in \mathcal{M}$. Likewise, the set of distributions that satisfy the identities (5.1) is convex.

::: proof
The conditions $\mathbb{E}_\mu[g\circ\Phi^t] = \mathbb{E}_\mu[g]$ and $\mathbb{E}_\mu[\mathcal{L}\varphi] = 0$ are linear in $\mu$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.15 — Ergodic measures are the extreme points]{.tag}
An invariant measure is ergodic if and only if it cannot be written as $p\,\mu_1 + (1 - p)\,\mu_2$ with $0 < p < 1$ and invariant $\mu_1 \ne \mu_2$.

::: proof
If $\mu$ is not ergodic, there exists an invariant set $A$ with $0 < \mu(A) < 1$. The conditional measures $\mu_A = \mu(\cdot\cap A)/\mu(A)$ and $\mu_{A^c} = \mu(\cdot\cap A^c)/\mu(A^c)$ are invariant (because $A$ and its complement are), distinct (one gives mass to $A$, the other does not), and $\mu = \mu(A)\,\mu_A + (1 - \mu(A))\,\mu_{A^c}$: $\mu$ is not extreme. Conversely (sketch), if $\mu$ is ergodic and $\mu = p\mu_1 + (1-p)\mu_2$, then $\mu_1 \le \mu/p$ has a density $h$ with respect to $\mu$; the invariance of $\mu$ and $\mu_1$ implies that $h$ is an invariant function, hence constant by ergodicity, and $\mu_1 = \mu$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.16 — Symmetry and mixtures]{.tag}
Suppose the system is equivariant under $S$ (definition 3.10) and let $\mu^+$ be an invariant measure. Then $\mu^- = S_\#\mu^+$, the image of $\mu^+$ under $S$ (the distribution of $SX$ when $X \sim \mu^+$), is invariant, and all the mixtures

$$
\mu_p = p\,\mu^+ + (1 - p)\,\mu^-, \qquad p \in [0, 1],
$$

are invariant and satisfy **all** the identities (5.1). If $\mu^+ \ne \mu^-$, the stationarity identities therefore do not determine the weight $p$.

::: proof
By definition 3.10, $\Phi^t\circ S = S\circ\Phi^t$. For bounded continuous $g$, $\mathbb{E}_{\mu^-}[g\circ\Phi^t] = \mathbb{E}_{\mu^+}[g\circ\Phi^t\circ S] = \mathbb{E}_{\mu^+}[g\circ S\circ\Phi^t] = \mathbb{E}_{\mu^+}[g\circ S] = \mathbb{E}_{\mu^-}[g]$, using the invariance of $\mu^+$ for the function $g\circ S$. The mixtures are invariant by proposition 5.14, and theorem 5.11 applies to each of them. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Here is the consequence for the internship. Below the crisis threshold (for $0.80 \le \Gamma \le 0.86$ in the Gissinger model with $\mu = 0.119$, according to experiment E1 and the simulations of chapter 7), there are two separate attractors and, we assume, two ergodic physical measures $\mu^+_\Gamma$ (positive dipole) and $\mu^-_\Gamma = S_\#\mu^+_\Gamma$. No stationarity identity can tell whether the data should be split half and half, three quarters to one quarter, or entirely on one side: this weight is set by the distribution of the initial conditions, that is, by the way the data were produced. Above the threshold, the attractor is unique and symmetric, and the weight is determined (the fraction of time spent with $D > 0$ tends to $1/2$).

The last part of the previous code illustrates exactly this point at $\Gamma = 0.84$: out of 40 trajectories, 15 are on the attractor $D > 0$; the mixtures $p = 1$, $0.75$, $0.5$ and $0$ have very different means $\mathbb{E}[D]$ (from $+1.07$ to $-1.07$), but their six residuals all remain of order $10^{-2}$, that is, at the level of the sampling noise. The identities do not see the difference.

::: note
[Remark 5.17 — Two consequences for a generative model]{.tag}
*(i)* The Dirac masses at the fixed points also satisfy (5.1), since $F(\mathbf{x}^*) = \mathbf{0}$ cancels $F\cdot\nabla\varphi$: a model that collapsed onto $N_+$ would satisfy the constraint perfectly. The stationarity identities must therefore be combined with a data-fidelity term; this is also what is noted by the works that learn dynamics from invariant measures, where the non-uniqueness of these measures is explicitly pointed out (Schiff et al., 2024). (ii) With non-degenerate noise, the stationary distribution is unique; if the system is symmetric, its image under $S$ is again stationary, hence equal to itself: **the noise selects the symmetric mixture** $p = 1/2$. Exercise 15 checks this on the double well, where all particles start from the same well and yet end up split equally between the two.
:::

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 5
:::
- An invariant measure is a distribution preserved by the flow; one always exists on a trapping region (Krylov–Bogoliubov), and often infinitely many.
- Birkhoff: for an ergodic measure, time average = ensemble average; the physical (SRB) measure is the one seen by typical initial conditions; for a dissipative system, it has no density.
- Liouville: $\partial_t\rho + \nabla\cdot(\rho F) = 0$; Fokker–Planck: $\partial_t\rho = -\nabla\cdot(\rho F) + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\Delta\rho$; generator $\mathcal{L}\varphi = F\cdot\nabla\varphi + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\Delta\varphi$.
- Stationary weak form: $\mathbb{E}_\mu[\mathcal{L}\varphi] = 0$ for every test function, proved through time averages without any density assumption; the energy budget is the case $\varphi = E$.
- Invariant measures form a convex set whose extreme points are the ergodic measures; the identities do not fix the relative weight of two symmetric attractors, and are also satisfied by the Dirac masses at the fixed points.
::::

## 6. Noise-induced transitions: Kramers and Rice {#ch6}

In the VKS experiment, the magnetic field reverses irregularly within a turbulent flow (Berhanu et al., 2007). Two mechanisms can produce such reversals: deterministic chaotic dynamics after a crisis (chapter 4), or fluctuations, modeled by a noise, that drive the system over a barrier between two stable states (Pétrélis et al., 2009). This chapter treats the second mechanism on the simplest model, then gives a tool common to both: the Rice formula, which computes a crossing frequency from the stationary distribution alone.

### 6.1 The noisy double well

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Double well]{.tag}
We consider $\mathrm{d}X = -U'(X)\,\mathrm{d}t + \sigma\,\mathrm{d}W$ with the potential $U(x) = x^4/4 - x^2/2$. Its minima are $x = \pm 1$, with $U(\pm 1) = -1/4$ and $U''(\pm 1) = 2$; its local maximum is the saddle $x = 0$, with $U(0) = 0$ and $U''(0) = -1$. The **barrier** is $\Delta U = U(0) - U(\pm 1) = 1/4$.
:::

Without noise, this is a frozen supercritical pitchfork (proposition 3.6 with $r = 1$): two symmetric stable states $\pm 1$, the analog of $\pm\mathbf{B}$. With noise, the particle fluctuates in one well and, from time to time, crosses the saddle. Its stationary distribution is $\rho \propto e^{-2U/\sigma^2}$ (proposition 5.10), bimodal and symmetric.

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.2 — Mean first-passage time]{.tag}
Let $\tau(x)$ be the mean time taken, starting from $x$, to reach a point $\beta > x$. Then $\tau$ satisfies $\mathcal{L}\tau = -1$, i.e. $\frac{\sigma^2}{2}\tau'' - U'\tau' = -1$, with $\tau(\beta) = 0$, and

$$
\tau(x) = \frac{2}{\sigma^2}\int_x^\beta e^{2U(y)/\sigma^2}\Big(\int_{-\infty}^y e^{-2U(z)/\sigma^2}\,\mathrm{d}z\Big)\mathrm{d}y . \tag{6.1}
$$

::: proof
Equation (heuristic “first-step” argument). During a short interval $\Delta t$, the particle moves from $x$ to $x + \delta X$; the remaining time is then on average $\tau(x + \delta X)$. Hence $\tau(x) = \Delta t + \mathbb{E}[\tau(x + \delta X)] = \Delta t + \tau(x) + \Delta t\,\mathcal{L}\tau(x) + o(\Delta t)$ by proposition 5.8, whence $\mathcal{L}\tau = -1$. The condition $\tau(\beta) = 0$ is obvious. On the left, there is no boundary: the confining potential sends the particle back, and we impose that $e^{-2U(y)/\sigma^2}\tau'(y)$ tend to $0$ as $y \to -\infty$ (this is the case as soon as $\tau'$ remains bounded; the solution below even satisfies $\tau'(y) \approx -1/|U'(y)| \to 0$).

Solving the equation. Multiply it by $\frac{2}{\sigma^2}e^{-2U/\sigma^2}$; the left-hand side becomes an exact derivative: $\big(e^{-2U/\sigma^2}\tau'\big)' = -\frac{2}{\sigma^2}e^{-2U/\sigma^2}$. Integrating from $-\infty$ to $y$, $\tau'(y) = -\frac{2}{\sigma^2}e^{2U(y)/\sigma^2}\int_{-\infty}^y e^{-2U(z)/\sigma^2}\,\mathrm{d}z$, then we integrate from $x$ to $\beta$ with $\tau(\beta) = 0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.3 — Arrhenius–Kramers law]{.tag}
As $\sigma \to 0$, the mean time to go from the minimum $x_- = -1$ to the opposite minimum is asymptotically equivalent to

$$
\tau_K = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{U''(x_-)\,|U''(0)|}}\;\exp\Big(\frac{2\,\Delta U}{\sigma^2}\Big). \tag{6.2}
$$

For our potential, $\tau_K = \pi\sqrt2\;e^{1/(2\sigma^2)}$.

::: proof
We apply Laplace's method to (6.1) with $x = -1$ and $\beta = +1$. The factor $e^{2U(y)/\sigma^2}$ is maximal at the saddle $y = 0$, and very sharply peaked when $\sigma$ is small: $\int_{-1}^{1}e^{2U(y)/\sigma^2}\,\mathrm{d}y \approx e^{2U(0)/\sigma^2}\sqrt{\pi\sigma^2/|U''(0)|}$ (Gaussian integral of $e^{-|U''(0)|y^2/\sigma^2}$). For $y$ close to $0$, the inner integral is dominated by the minimum $z = -1$: $\int_{-\infty}^y e^{-2U(z)/\sigma^2}\,\mathrm{d}z \approx e^{-2U(-1)/\sigma^2}\sqrt{\pi\sigma^2/U''(-1)}$. The product, multiplied by $2/\sigma^2$, gives

$$
\frac{2}{\sigma^2}\cdot\frac{\pi\sigma^2}{\sqrt{U''(-1)\,|U''(0)|}}\,e^{2(U(0) - U(-1))/\sigma^2} = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{U''(-1)\,|U''(0)|}}\,e^{2\Delta U/\sigma^2}.
$$

With $U''(-1) = 2$, $|U''(0)| = 1$ and $\Delta U = 1/4$, we find $\pi\sqrt2\,e^{1/(2\sigma^2)}$. If we stopped at the saddle ($\beta = 0$), we would integrate only half of the Gaussian, and the time would be $\tau_K/2$: once at the saddle, the particle has a one-in-two chance of falling back to the starting side. Rigorous proofs, valid in any dimension for reversible diffusions (Eyring–Kramers formula), are due to Bovier et al. (2004); Berglund (2013) gives a review. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

With the diffusion coefficient $\mathcal{D} = \sigma^2/2$, the exponent reads $\Delta U/\mathcal{D}$: this is the Arrhenius law $e^{\Delta E/k_BT}$ of chemical reactions, which Kramers (1940) derived from a diffusion model; Hänggi, Talkner and Borkovec (1990) review its history and developments. The mean time grows **exponentially** as the noise decreases: halving $\sigma^2$ squares the time, up to the prefactor.

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.4 — Exponential residence times]{.tag}
If the probability of leaving a well during $[t, t + \mathrm{d}t]$, given that the particle is still there, equals $k\,\mathrm{d}t$ with a constant rate $k$, then the residence time $T$ follows an exponential distribution: $\mathbb{P}(T > t) = e^{-kt}$, with mean $1/k$ and standard deviation $1/k$.

::: proof
Let $G(t) = \mathbb{P}(T > t)$. Staying until $t + \mathrm{d}t$ means staying until $t$ and then not leaving: $G(t + \mathrm{d}t) = G(t)(1 - k\,\mathrm{d}t)$, whence $G' = -kG$ and $G(t) = e^{-kt}$. The mean and variance of an exponential distribution with parameter $k$ are $1/k$ and $1/k^2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The constant-rate assumption is justified when the barrier is high: the particle relaxes in its well in a time of order $1$, much shorter than $\tau_K$, and “forgets” its past before each attempt. The reversals then approximately form a **Poisson process**; this is the statistics observed for the long polarity intervals of the Gissinger model (Gissinger, 2012) and predicted by the noisy model of Pétrélis et al. (2009), whose mean time has precisely the Kramers form: a prefactor multiplied by the exponential of the ratio between the barrier and the noise intensity.

The following code simulates the double well for four noise levels and compares the simulated mean switching time, the exact formula (6.1) and the asymptotic formula (6.2).

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import quad
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

# Double well U(x) = x^4/4 - x^2/2: minima at ±1, saddle at 0, barrier dU = 1/4
U = lambda x: x**4 / 4 - x**2 / 2
dU = 0.25

def tau_exact(s):
    """Mean first-passage time from -1 to +1 (exact integral formula in dimension 1)."""
    inner = lambda y: quad(lambda z: np.exp(-2 * U(z) / s**2), -np.inf, y)[0]
    return 2 / s**2 * quad(lambda y: np.exp(2 * U(y) / s**2) * inner(y), -1, 1)[0]

def tau_kramers(s):
    """Arrhenius-Kramers law: 2 pi / sqrt(U''(-1) |U''(0)|) * exp(2 dU / s^2)."""
    return 2 * np.pi / np.sqrt(2.0 * 1.0) * np.exp(2 * dU / s**2)

# Euler-Maruyama dX = -U'(X) dt + s dW for four values of s at once (250 particles each)
niveaux = np.array([0.40, 0.45, 0.50, 0.60])
sig = np.repeat(niveaux, 250)
dt, T = 0.01, 800.0
x = -np.ones(sig.size)
puits = -np.ones(sig.size)            # last minimum reached (-1 or +1)
t_entree = np.zeros(sig.size)
nb = np.zeros(sig.size)               # number of switches from one minimum to the other
sejours = [[] for _ in sig]           # complete residence times (excluding the first residence)
for k in range(int(T / dt)):
    x += -(x**3 - x) * dt + sig * np.sqrt(dt) * rng.standard_normal(sig.size)
    bascule = ((puits < 0) & (x > 1)) | ((puits > 0) & (x < -1))
    for i in np.flatnonzero(bascule):
        if nb[i] > 0:
            sejours[i].append((k + 1) * dt - t_entree[i])
        t_entree[i], puits[i], nb[i] = (k + 1) * dt, -puits[i], nb[i] + 1

print("  s   | switches | tau (sim.) | tau exact | tau Kramers | std deviation/mean | P(T > 2 tau)")
for s in niveaux:
    i = np.flatnonzero(sig == s)
    m = i.size * T / nb[i].sum()                 # total observed time / number of switches
    tt = np.concatenate([sejours[j] for j in i])
    print(f" {s:.2f} | {int(nb[i].sum()):8d} | {m:10.1f} | {tau_exact(s):9.1f} | {tau_kramers(s):11.1f} |"
          f" {tt.std() / tt.mean():18.2f} | {np.mean(tt > 2 * tt.mean()):.3f}")

# Arrhenius law: slope of ln(tau) as a function of 1/s^2, expected 2 dU = 0.5 as s -> 0
for a, b in [(0.6, 0.4), (0.25, 0.2), (0.15, 0.125)]:
    p = (np.log(tau_exact(b)) - np.log(tau_exact(a))) / (1 / b**2 - 1 / a**2)
    print(f"slope (exact formula) between s = {a} and s = {b}: {p:.3f}")
# output:
#   s   | switches | tau (sim.) | tau exact | tau Kramers | std deviation/mean | P(T > 2 tau)
#  0.40 |     1659 |      120.6 |     120.0 |       101.1 |               0.96 | 0.136
#  0.45 |     3021 |       66.2 |      64.4 |        52.5 |               0.92 | 0.127
#  0.50 |     4866 |       41.1 |      41.0 |        32.8 |               0.92 | 0.124
#  0.60 |     9107 |       22.0 |      22.2 |        17.8 |               0.90 | 0.120
# slope (exact formula) between s = 0.6 and s = 0.4: 0.486
# slope (exact formula) between s = 0.25 and s = 0.2: 0.497
# slope (exact formula) between s = 0.15 and s = 0.125: 0.500
```

The simulation and the exact formula agree to within 3% (the residual discrepancy comes from the Euler–Maruyama time step and the finite number of switches). The Kramers asymptotics underestimates the time by 16 to 20% at these noise levels: its corrections are of relative order $\sigma^2/\Delta U$, which is not small here ($\Delta U/\mathcal{D}$ lies between $1.4$ and $3.1$). The slope of $\ln\tau$ as a function of $1/\sigma^2$ does tend to $2\Delta U = 0.5$ as $\sigma \to 0$. Finally, the ratio of standard deviation to mean is close to $1$ and $\mathbb{P}(T > 2\tau)$ close to $e^{-2} \approx 0.135$, as for an exponential distribution; the slight deficit comes from the deterministic part of each residence (the descent from the saddle to the minimum), which is not random.

![Noisy double well. (a) Potential U(x) = x⁴/4 − x²/2, with its two minima at ±1 and the barrier ΔU = 1/4 at the saddle x = 0. (b) A trajectory for σ = 0.45: the particle fluctuates around −1 or +1 and switches at irregular times. (c) Mean switching time as a function of 1/σ² on a logarithmic scale: exact formula (solid line), Kramers asymptotics (dashes, parallel but lower) and simulations (disks), aligned on a straight line with slope close to 2ΔU = 0.5.](../../../prep/p4-systemes-dynamiques/figures/kramers-en.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Three panels. On the left, a W-shaped curve with two troughs at minus 0.25 at x equal minus 1 and plus 1, and a vertical arrow indicating the barrier of 1/4. In the middle, a noisy signal alternating between plateaus around minus 1 and plus 1, with about ten switches over 600 time units. On the right, on a logarithmic scale, two nearly parallel lines rising from 10 to 1000 as 1 over sigma squared goes from 2 to 11, the exact curve above the Kramers dashes, and four green disks lying on the exact curve."}

### 6.2 The Rice formula

Experiment E1 seeks to predict the reversal frequency from a generative model that only produces **samples of the stationary distribution**, without any temporal information. This is possible thanks to a formula of Rice (1944, 1945).

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.5 — Rice formula]{.tag}
Let $X(t)$ be a stationary process with trajectories of class $C^1$, such that the pair $(X(t), \dot X(t))$ has a joint density $p(x, \dot x)$ continuous in $x$ near $0$ (and under technical regularity assumptions). The mean number of zero crossings per unit time is

$$
\nu_0 = \int_{\mathbb{R}}|\dot x|\,p(0, \dot x)\,\mathrm{d}\dot x = \mathbb{E}\big[|\dot X|\,\delta(X)\big]. \tag{6.3}
$$

::: proof
Heuristic proof. *Kac's counting formula.* Let $x(t)$ be a function of class $C^1$ whose zeros $t_k$ in $[0, T]$ are simple ($\dot x(t_k) \ne 0$). For small $h$, near each $t_k$, the function crosses the band $\{|x| < h\}$ monotonically, in a time $\approx 2h/|\dot x(t_k)|$. Hence

$$
\frac{1}{2h}\int_0^T \mathbf{1}_{\{|x(t)| < h\}}\,|\dot x(t)|\,\mathrm{d}t \;\longrightarrow\; \sum_k \frac{1}{2h}\cdot\frac{2h}{|\dot x(t_k)|}\cdot|\dot x(t_k)| = N_{[0,T]},
$$

the number of zeros. *Taking expectations.* We take the expectation, exchange limit and expectation (this is the technical step) and use stationarity: $\mathbb{E}[N_{[0,T]}] = T\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{2h}\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbf{1}_{\{|X| < h\}}|\dot X|\big] = T\int|\dot x|\,p(0, \dot x)\,\mathrm{d}\dot x$. A rigorous proof can be found in Azaïs and Wschebor (2009). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Corollary 6.6 — Stationary Gaussian process]{.tag}
If $X$ is Gaussian, centered, stationary, with a twice-differentiable covariance $C(\tau) = \mathbb{E}[X(t)X(t+\tau)]$, then

$$
\nu_0 = \frac{1}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{-C''(0)}{C(0)}} = \frac{\sigma_{\dot X}}{\pi\,\sigma_X}.
$$

::: proof
By stationarity, $\mathbb{E}[X\dot X] = \frac12\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}[X^2] = 0$: $X(t)$ and $\dot X(t)$, jointly Gaussian and uncorrelated, are independent. Moreover $\operatorname{Var}\dot X = -C''(0)$. Hence $p(0, \dot x) = p_X(0)\,p_{\dot X}(\dot x)$, with $p_X(0) = 1/(\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma_X)$ and $\mathbb{E}|\dot X| = \sigma_{\dot X}\sqrt{2/\pi}$. The product equals $\sigma_{\dot X}/(\pi\sigma_X)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Remark 6.7 — Domain of validity and use in the internship]{.tag}
The formula requires differentiable trajectories. It does not apply to Brownian motion or to the noisy double well, whose trajectories cross zero infinitely many times in the neighborhood of each crossing; this is why, above, we counted the switches from one minimum to the other (between $-1$ and $+1$), and not the zero crossings. The Gissinger model, on the other hand, is deterministic and $D(t)$ is of class $C^1$; at $D = 0$, its derivative is $\dot D = -\nu D + VQ = VQ$, whence

$$
\nu_0 = \mathbb{E}_{\mu_\Gamma}\big[|VQ|\,\delta(D)\big] \approx \frac{1}{2h}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mu_\Gamma}\big[|{-\nu D} + VQ|\,\mathbf{1}_{\{|D| < h\}}\big],
$$

a quantity that can be computed on generated samples without temporal order. The choice of $h$ trades off bias (which grows with $h$) against variance (which grows as $h$ decreases, since few samples fall in the window). Finally, $\nu_0$ counts **all** zero crossings: a reversal produces one, an excursion (the dipole crosses zero and then comes back) produces two.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)

# 1) Smooth stationary Gaussian process: sum of 200 cosines with random phases
K = 200
w = rng.uniform(0.5, 3.0, K)                    # angular frequencies
a = rng.normal(size=K) / np.sqrt(K)             # amplitudes
ph = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, K)
t = np.arange(0, 2000, 0.01)
X = np.zeros_like(t); Xp = np.zeros_like(t)
for wk, ak, pk in zip(w, a, ph):
    X += ak * np.cos(wk * t + pk)
    Xp -= ak * wk * np.sin(wk * t + pk)
compte = np.sum(np.sign(X[1:]) != np.sign(X[:-1])) / t[-1]
m0, m2 = np.sum(a**2) / 2, np.sum(a**2 * w**2) / 2  # variances of X and of dX/dt
h = 0.02
rice_ech = np.mean(np.abs(Xp) * (np.abs(X) < h)) / (2 * h)
print(f"Gaussian: direct count = {compte:.4f} ; Rice on sample = {rice_ech:.4f} ;"
      f" formula sqrt(m2/m0)/pi = {np.sqrt(m2 / m0) / np.pi:.4f}")

# 2) Gissinger model, Gamma = 0.9: zero crossings of D
mu, nu, G = 0.119, 0.1, 0.9
f = lambda Y: np.array([mu * Y[0] - Y[2] * Y[1], -nu * Y[1] + Y[2] * Y[0], G - Y[2] + Y[0] * Y[1]])
Y = rng.normal(size=(3, 40)) * 0.8; Y[2] = np.abs(Y[2])
dt = 0.02
for _ in range(int(300 / dt)):                     # transient
    k1 = f(Y); k2 = f(Y + dt/2*k1); k3 = f(Y + dt/2*k2); k4 = f(Y + dt*k3)
    Y = Y + dt / 6 * (k1 + 2*k2 + 2*k3 + k4)
passages, echant, duree = 0, [], 1200.0
for k in range(int(duree / dt)):
    s0 = np.sign(Y[1])
    k1 = f(Y); k2 = f(Y + dt/2*k1); k3 = f(Y + dt/2*k2); k4 = f(Y + dt*k3)
    Y = Y + dt / 6 * (k1 + 2*k2 + 2*k3 + k4)
    passages += np.sum(np.sign(Y[1]) != s0)
    if k % 10 == 0:                                # one sample every 0.2 time unit
        echant.append(Y.T.copy())
S = np.concatenate(echant)
S = S[rng.permutation(len(S))]                     # forget the temporal order: only the distribution matters
Q, D, V = S.T
taux = passages / (40 * duree)
print(f"Gissinger: {passages} crossings, measured rate = {taux:.5f} per unit time")
for h in (0.4, 0.2, 0.1):
    r = np.mean(np.abs(-nu * D + V * Q) * (np.abs(D) < h)) / (2 * h)
    print(f"  Rice from the distribution alone (h = {h}): {r:.5f} ; P(|D| < h) = {np.mean(np.abs(D) < h):.4f}")
# output:
# Gaussian: direct count = 0.6125 ; Rice on sample = 0.6163 ; formula sqrt(m2/m0)/pi = 0.6041
# Gissinger: 203 crossings, measured rate = 0.00423 per unit time
#   Rice from the distribution alone (h = 0.4): 0.00418 ; P(|D| < h) = 0.0070
#   Rice from the distribution alone (h = 0.2): 0.00414 ; P(|D| < h) = 0.0024
#   Rice from the distribution alone (h = 0.1): 0.00438 ; P(|D| < h) = 0.0012
```

For the Gaussian process, the direct count, formula (6.3) evaluated on the sample and the closed-form formula of corollary 6.6 agree to within 2%; the discrepancy with the closed form comes from the fact that a sum of 200 cosines with fixed amplitudes is only approximately Gaussian and that a single realization is observed. For the Gissinger model at $\Gamma = 0.9$, the Rice formula applied to the **shuffled** samples (the temporal order was destroyed by the permutation) recovers the measured rate to within 1 to 4%. It relies on a very small fraction of the distribution: only 0.24% of the samples have $|D| < 0.2$. A generative model must therefore represent faithfully a region of very low probability in order to predict the reversal frequency correctly.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 6
:::
- Double well $U = x^4/4 - x^2/2$: stationary distribution $\rho \propto e^{-2U/\sigma^2}$, bimodal and symmetric.
- Mean first-passage time: solution of $\mathcal{L}\tau = -1$, integral formula (6.1), exact in dimension 1.
- Arrhenius–Kramers law: $\tau \approx \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{U''(x_-)|U''(x_s)|}}\,e^{2\Delta U/\sigma^2}$; exponential growth as the noise decreases; corrections of order $\sigma^2/\Delta U$.
- Constant escape rate: exponential residence times, Poissonian reversals.
- Rice formula: $\nu_0 = \mathbb{E}[|\dot X|\,\delta(X)]$ for a smooth stationary process; $\sigma_{\dot X}/(\pi\sigma_X)$ in the Gaussian case; for Gissinger, $\nu_0 = \mathbb{E}[|VQ|\,\delta(D)]$, computable from the distribution alone.
::::

## 7. The Gissinger model, the common thread of the internship {#ch7}

The three-mode model of Gissinger (2012) brings the whole module together: a symmetry $\mathbf{B} \mapsto -\mathbf{B}$, unstable fixed points, a chaotic attractor, a merging crisis that gives rise to reversals, an invariant distribution that changes nature at the threshold. It is the first test bed of the internship (experiment E1, see the [report](../../rapport/index.html#e1)): the distribution $\mu_\Gamma$ conditioned on $\Gamma$ is learned there with a flow matching model, and we check what this model respects of the physics.

### 7.1 The model and its properties

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Gissinger model (2012)]{.tag}
The quadrupole $Q$, the dipole $D$ and a velocity mode $V$ obey

$$
\dot Q = \mu Q - VD, \qquad \dot D = -\nu D + VQ, \qquad \dot V = \Gamma - V + QD,
$$

with $\mu = 0.119$ and $\nu = 0.1$ fixed and the forcing $\Gamma$ as the control parameter. According to Gissinger (2012), $V$ represents a flow mode that breaks the mirror symmetry with respect to the equatorial plane, sustained by the forcing $\Gamma$, and the term $QD$ in the third equation represents the feedback of the Lorentz force; $V$ does not change sign during reversals. In the 2010 paper (Gissinger, Dormy and Fauve), the roles of $D$ and $Q$ are swapped; here we follow the 2012 convention, which is that of experiment E1.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.2 — Symmetry, dissipation, fixed points]{.tag}
*(i)* The system is equivariant under $S : (Q, D, V) \mapsto (-Q, -D, V)$, the image of $\mathbf{B} \mapsto -\mathbf{B}$. (ii) Its divergence equals $\mu - \nu - 1 = -0.981$: it contracts volumes. (iii) For $\mu = 0.119$, $\nu = 0.1$ and $\Gamma$ between $0.8$ and $1$, its fixed points are $O = (0, 0, \Gamma)$, a weakly unstable focus, and $N_\pm$, unstable saddle-foci; the points $M_\pm$ do not exist.

::: proof
*(i)* $F(-Q, -D, V) = \big({-\mu Q} + VD,\ \nu D - VQ,\ \Gamma - V + QD\big) = S\,F(Q, D, V)$. (ii) The trace of the Jacobian of example 2.7 equals $\mu - \nu - 1$. (iii) Computation of example 2.7: at $O$, the real part $(\mu - \nu)/2 = 0.0095$ is positive and the discriminant $(\mu + \nu)^2 - 4\Gamma^2$ is negative as soon as $\Gamma > 0.11$; $M_\pm$ would require $\sqrt{\mu\nu} \approx 0.109 > \Gamma$. For $N_\pm$ at $\Gamma = 0.9$, the code of chapter 2 gives the eigenvalues $-1.17$ and $0.094 \pm 0.607\,i$; rerunning this code for $\Gamma = 0.80$ and $\Gamma = 1.00$, we obtain $0.088 \pm 0.579\,i$ and $0.100 \pm 0.632\,i$ (with a third eigenvalue close to $-1.17$): the real part remains positive over the whole range. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 7.2 The reversal threshold

Gissinger (2012) describes the scenario as $\mu$ decreases, at fixed $\Gamma = 0.9$ and $\nu = 0.1$: stationary states $N_\pm$ for $\mu > 0.2$, then a periodic orbit around each $N_\pm$, a period-doubling cascade below $\mu \approx 0.138$, and finally the merging crisis at $\mu_c \approx 0.11928$. At $\mu = 0.12$, the chaos remains confined around a single fixed point, without reversal; at $\mu = 0.119$, the reversals are chaotic, with a Lyapunov exponent $\lambda \simeq 0.1$. The waiting times between reversals are quantized at short times (influence of the unstable periodic orbits) and Poissonian at long times.

Experiment E1 of this repository fixes $\mu = 0.119$ and varies $\Gamma$ between $0.80$ and $1.00$. The reversal threshold is **observed numerically between $\Gamma = 0.86$ and $\Gamma = 0.865$**: on the fine grid of step $0.005$, no zero crossing of $D$ for $\Gamma \le 0.86$, crossings from $0.865$ on (see the [report](../../rapport/index.html#e1)). The following code repeats this sweep, with 30 trajectories of 1,500 time units per value of $\Gamma$, after a transient of 600 units.

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

mu, nu = 0.119, 0.1
gammas = np.array([0.84, 0.85, 0.86, 0.865, 0.87, 0.88, 0.90, 0.95])
n_traj = 30
g = np.repeat(gammas, n_traj)                       # one value of Gamma per trajectory

def f(Y):
    q, d, v = Y
    return np.array([mu * q - v * d, -nu * d + v * q, g - v + q * d])

def pas(Y, dt):
    k1 = f(Y); k2 = f(Y + dt/2*k1); k3 = f(Y + dt/2*k2); k4 = f(Y + dt*k3)
    return Y + dt / 6 * (k1 + 2*k2 + 2*k3 + k4)

Y = rng.normal(size=(3, g.size)) * 0.8; Y[2] = np.abs(Y[2])
dt, t_trans, duree = 0.02, 600.0, 1500.0   # long transient: O is a barely unstable focus
for _ in range(int(t_trans / dt)):
    Y = pas(Y, dt)
passages = np.zeros(g.size)
temps_positif = np.zeros(g.size)
for _ in range(int(duree / dt)):
    s0 = np.sign(Y[1])
    Y = pas(Y, dt)
    passages += np.sign(Y[1]) != s0
    temps_positif += Y[1] > 0

print("Gamma | crossings | rate (per unit of t) | trajectories that changed sign | P(D > 0)")
for G in gammas:
    i = g == G
    print(f"{G:5.3f} | {int(passages[i].sum()):8d} | {passages[i].sum() / (n_traj * duree):21.5f} |"
          f" {int((passages[i] > 0).sum()):17d} / {n_traj} | {temps_positif[i].sum() / (n_traj * duree / dt):.3f}")
# output:
# Gamma | crossings | rate (per unit of t) | trajectories that changed sign | P(D > 0)
# 0.840 |        0 |               0.00000 |                 0 / 30 | 0.600
# 0.850 |        0 |               0.00000 |                 0 / 30 | 0.600
# 0.860 |        0 |               0.00000 |                 0 / 30 | 0.467
# 0.865 |       61 |               0.00136 |                29 / 30 | 0.526
# 0.870 |       91 |               0.00202 |                27 / 30 | 0.403
# 0.880 |      163 |               0.00362 |                30 / 30 | 0.509
# 0.900 |      186 |               0.00413 |                30 / 30 | 0.445
# 0.950 |      386 |               0.00858 |                30 / 30 | 0.514
```

The result is consistent with E1: no crossing up to $\Gamma = 0.86$, crossings for almost all trajectories from $\Gamma = 0.865$ on. The rate then grows with $\Gamma$. Below the threshold, the fraction of time spent with $D > 0$ equals $0.60$, $0.60$ or $0.47$ depending on the draws: it only reflects the distribution of the initial conditions between the two attractors, as proposition 5.16 announced. Above it, it fluctuates around $1/2$.

Two numerical precautions are needed. First, the transient must be long: a trajectory starting near the axis $D = Q = 0$ revolves around the focus $O$, whose instability rate is only $0.0095$, and its zero crossings during this phase are an artifact of the transient, not reversals (with a transient of only 300 units, one trajectory out of 30 at $\Gamma = 0.84$ still produced about ten). Second, just above a crisis, the mean time between switches diverges (example 4.8): a finite simulation can miss very rare switches, and the exact position of the threshold depends slightly on the observed duration and on the integration step. We therefore retain $0.86 < \Gamma_c \le 0.865$ for this integration (RK4, step $0.02$), compatible with the interval $]0.86\,;\,0.87]$ of E1.

![The Gissinger model (μ = 0.119, ν = 0.1) on either side of the crisis. (a) D(t) at Γ = 0.86 for two trajectories starting from symmetric initial conditions: each stays on its own side, without reversal. (b) D(t) at Γ = 0.90: long polarity intervals interrupted by irregular reversals. (c) Projection (Q, D) at Γ = 0.84: two disjoint attractors, images of each other under the symmetry S. (d) Projection at Γ = 0.90: a single symmetric attractor, with the corridors leading from one polarity to the other. (e) Rate of zero crossings of D as a function of Γ, measured by the code above: zero up to 0.86, positive from 0.865 on.](../../../prep/p4-systemes-dynamiques/figures/gissinger-en.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Five panels. Top left, two oscillating signals, one around plus 1 in orange, the other around minus 1 in blue, which never cross over 1500 time units. Bottom left, a blue signal that stays for several hundred time units around minus 1 or plus 1 and jumps from one to the other about eight times. Top center, two crescent-shaped point clouds, one at the top left in orange, the other at the bottom right in blue, without contact. Top right, a single blue cloud that combines the two crescents and connects them by arcs. Bottom right, a rate curve that is zero for Gamma from 0.84 to 0.86 and then increases up to 0.0086 at Gamma equal 0.95, with an orange band between 0.86 and 0.865 marking the threshold."}
